# Overview


This page introduces **DeepSpot-M**, a research codebase for predicting gene expression directly from histology images. It explains what the model does, how its architecture fits together at a high level, what ships inside this repository, and how to install and run your first prediction — everything a beginner needs before diving deeper. For hands-on setup, continue to [Quick Start](2-quick-start).

## What Is DeepSpot-M?

DeepSpot-M is a **multimodal foundation model for transcriptome-wide virtual spatial transcriptomics**. In practical terms: you give it a small patch of an H&E-stained tissue image (a 224×224 pixel tile), and it returns predicted expression levels across a panel of roughly **19,000 genes** — effectively "reading out" the molecular state of the tissue from how it looks under a microscope.

The key design insight is that **genes are represented as queryable embeddings rather than fixed outputs**. Each gene query attends to the image's patch tokens through a cross-attention decoder, and a *gene router hypernetwork* generates gene-specific output projections from frozen biological embeddings drawn from five foundation models covering different modalities: Evo 2 (DNA), Orthrus (RNA), ProtT5 (protein), scGPT (single-cell), and Apertus (text). Because gene identity is an input rather than a hardwired output neuron, the model can even predict **genes it never saw during training** (zero-shot prediction).

![DeepSpot-M model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

The project comes with pretrained weights on Hugging Face, a Python package (`deepspotm` on PyPI), command-line prediction tools, a complete end-to-end tutorial, and a released **TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas** of 28,664 whole-slide images across 32 cancer types (295.3 million spots from 10,865 patients).

> ⚠️ **Research use only.** Not for clinical or diagnostic use.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L32), [README.md](README.md#L34-L44), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L15-L38)

## How It Works: Architecture at a Glance

The diagram below traces a single H&E tile through the four conceptual stages of the model. Before reading it, note that **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a technique that freezes a large pretrained model and trains only small adapter matrices — this lets the team adapt a pathology vision backbone cheaply — and a **hypernetwork** is a small network whose job is to generate the weights of another layer.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["224×224 H&E tile"] --> B["Image transforms<br/>(resize + normalize)"]
    B --> C["LoRA-adapted vision backbone<br/>(Midnight ViT)"]
    C --> D["Spatial patch tokens"]
    E["Gene queries<br/>(~19k genes)"] --> F["Cross-attention<br/>gene decoder"]
    D --> F
    G["Frozen biological gene embeddings<br/>(evo2 · orthrus · prott5 · scgpt · apertus)"] --> H["Gene router hypernetwork<br/>(per-gene output projection)"]
    F --> H
    H --> I["Predicted expression vector<br/>(1 × n_genes, log1p-CPM)"]
```

Reading the pipeline left to right:

1. **Vision stage** — the tile is resized/normalized, then tokenized into spatial patch tokens by a LoRA-adapted pathology foundation backbone. The released model uses the `MidnightEncoder` (ViT, embedding dim 1536) as the default; the code also ships adapters for UNI, UNI2, H-optimus-0/1, H0-mini, and CLIP through a shared encoder registry.
2. **Gene queries** — the vocabulary of ~19k gene names comes from a bundled `tokens.csv` asset; output column `i` of the forward pass always corresponds to `model.gene_names[i]`.
3. **Cross-attention decoder** — each gene query independently attends to the patch tokens via multi-head attention (2 layers, 8 heads, 256-dim gene embeddings by default), refining "what this gene should look like given this tissue."
4. **Gene router hypernetwork** — a small network reads each gene's frozen biological embedding and *generates* that gene's output projection weights and bias on the fly, producing the final scalar expression value.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L24-L32), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L40-L68), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L72-L111), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L111-L145), [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L301-L343), [config.py](src/deepspotm/config.py#L5-L19)

### Gene-Embedding Sources and Modalities

Each source is a different biological "prior" describing what genes are. At load time you pick **one** active source; the model collapses to that single pathway for efficient inference.

| Source | Modality | Foundation model origin |
|---|---|---|
| `evo2` | DNA | Genomic sequence model |
| `orthrus` | RNA | Transcriptomic sequence model |
| `prott5` | Protein | Protein language model |
| `scgpt` | single-cell | Single-cell expression model *(released default)* |
| `apertus` | text | Text foundation model |

Sources: [examples/predict.py](examples/predict.py#L2-L16), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L59-L88), [README.md](README.md#L24-L32)

## Key Capabilities

| Capability | What it means for you | Where to learn more |
|---|---|---|
| **Tile-level prediction** | One forward pass returns the full ~19k-gene expression vector per tile | [Quick Start](2-quick-start) |
| **Selective gene prediction** | `model.predict_genes(tile, ["EPCAM", ...])` computes only the requested gene queries — faster than the full panel | [Selective Gene Prediction](16-selective-gene-prediction) |
| **Whole-slide pipeline** | `predict_wsi.py` tiles an SVS-style slide, drops background, and writes a scanpy/squidpy-ready `.h5ad` | [Whole-Slide Image Pipeline](17-whole-slide-image-pipeline) |
| **Five gene-embedding sources** | Swap between evo2/orthrus/prott5/scgpt/apertus with one argument | [Multi-Source Gene Embeddings](11-multi-source-gene-embeddings) |
| **Zero-shot genes** | The router hypernetwork can score genes absent from training | [Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork) |
| **Self-contained checkpoints** | `from_pretrained` needs no download of the upstream backbone repo | [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading) |
| **Published atlas** | Ready-made predictions for 28,664 TCGA slides across 32 cancers | [Atlas and Dataset Access](5-atlas-and-dataset-access) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L65-L97), [README.md](README.md#L99-L121), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L370-L391)

## Repository Layout

The repository is deliberately compact — one installable package, a handful of examples, and a test suite:

```
DeepSpotM/
├── pyproject.toml          # packaging, dependencies, licenses
├── README.md               # project front page
├── assets/                 # model_overview.png used in docs
├── src/deepspotm/          # the installable package
│   ├── model.py            # DeepSpotM class: backbone + decoder assembly,
│   │                       #   from_pretrained, forward, predict_genes
│   ├── modules.py          # cross-attention decoder, gene router
│   │                       #   hypernetwork, multi-source embeddings
│   ├── image_encoder.py    # vision backbones (Midnight, UNI, H-optimus...)
│   ├── checkpoint.py       # state-dict loading & cross-vocabulary handling
│   ├── config.py           # paths to bundled gene vocabulary (tokens.csv)
│   ├── utils.py            # shared helpers (transforms, normalization)
│   └── assets/             # tokens.csv, midnight_config.json, mappings
├── examples/
│   ├── predict.py          # CLI: tile(s) → predictions / CSV
│   ├── predict_wsi.py      # CLI: whole slide → AnnData .h5ad
│   └── predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb  # end-to-end TCGA-SKCM tutorial
├── tests/                  # pytest suite (checkpoint, decoder, utils...)
└── LICENSE / WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md / THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md
```

The single public entry point `DeepSpotM` (plus the decoder, router, and loading utilities) is exported from the package root, so `from deepspotm import DeepSpotM` is all most users ever need to import.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L7-L14), [\_\_init\_\_.py](src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L1-L31), [config.py](src/deepspotm/config.py#L5-L19)

## Installation & Requirements

```bash
pip install deepspotm                # core package
pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"         # adds pyvips + anndata for predict_wsi.py
```

Python **3.10 or newer** is required — the core dependencies (torch, transformers, peft, lightning) no longer resolve on older versions.

| Dependency | Minimum | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `torch` | ≥ 2.0 | Tensor compute & model runtime |
| `lightning` | ≥ 2.0 | `LightningModule` base for `DeepSpotM` |
| `timm` | ≥ 0.9 | Builds timm-family vision backbones |
| `transformers` | ≥ 4.43 | Builds Midnight / CLIP backbones |
| `peft` | ≥ 0.6 | LoRA adapter wrapping of the backbone |
| `safetensors` | ≥ 0.3 | Weight file format |
| `huggingface_hub` | ≥ 0.20 | Downloads model files from the Hub |
| `pandas` / `numpy` / `pillow` | ≥ 2.0 / 1.24 / 9.0 | Vocabulary CSV, arrays, image I/O |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L46-L63), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L18-L29), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L46-L67)

## Your First Prediction

The minimal end-to-end flow is four steps: load the model, transform a tile, run the forward pass, and map the output vector back to gene symbols.

```python
from deepspotm import DeepSpotM

model, image_processor = DeepSpotM.from_pretrained(
    "ratschlab/DeepSpotM",
    source="scgpt",   # one of evo2, orthrus, prott5, scgpt, apertus
)

import torch
tile = image_processor(my_pil_tile).unsqueeze(0)   # 224x224 H&E tile
with torch.no_grad():
    expression, _, _ = model(tile)                 # (1, n_genes)

preds = dict(zip(model.gene_names, expression.squeeze(0).tolist()))
```

A few things worth noticing for beginners: `from_pretrained` returns the model **and** its matching image transform (normalization differs per backbone, so never skip it); the model is returned already on GPU (if available) and in eval mode; and because output column `i` is `model.gene_names[i]`, mapping predictions to gene symbols requires no extra vocabulary parsing.

> [!TIP]
> `from_pretrained` builds the Midnight backbone **offline** from a bundled config (`midnight_config.json`) and takes its weights entirely from the checkpoint — so loading works with no network access to the upstream `kaiko-ai/midnight` repo, and the released checkpoint is fully self-contained.

> [!TIP]
> For a handful of genes of interest (e.g. markers `BRAF`, `CD3D`, `COL1A1`), use `model.predict_genes(tile, genes)` instead of the full forward — only those gene queries are built and attended, which is measurably faster.

If you prefer not to write code at all, the bundled CLI tools cover the same workflows:

```bash
python examples/predict_wsi.py slide.svs -o slide.h5ad              # slide → .h5ad
python examples/predict.py tiles/ --genes EPCAM CD3D --output p.csv # tiles → CSV
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L65-L89), [README.md](README.md#L91-L97), [README.md](README.md#L99-L121), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L252-L331)

## Licensing & Usage Boundaries

The project uses a **split license**, which matters if you plan to redistribute anything:

| Artifact | License | Practical meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Source code | PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 | Non-commercial use only |
| Model weights | CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 | Non-commercial, ShareAlike, with attribution |
| Backbone & gene-embedding sources | MIT / Apache-2.0 | Permissive (see THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md) |

This is a research tool: predictions are estimates derived from image appearance and must not be used for clinical or diagnostic decisions. The package metadata itself encodes this stance (`license = "PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0"`).

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L7-L14), [README.md](README.md#L172-L183)

This documentation is organized as **Get Started** → **Deep Dive**. A productive route for a beginner:

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)** — environment setup and a working first run.
2. **[Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools)** — score tiles or whole slides without writing code.

6. Finally, the inference-engineering pages — starting with [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading) — explain how checkpoints, vocabularies, and memory-efficient loading fit together.


# Quick Start



This page takes you from an empty environment to your first predicted gene-expression profile. DeepSpot-M is a multimodal foundation model that maps a single 224×224 H&E histology tile to transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression (~19k genes): a LoRA-adapted pathology backbone tokenises the tile, each gene query attends to the patch tokens through a cross-attention decoder, and a gene router hypernetwork generates gene-specific output projections. Here you will install the package, load the published Hugging Face checkpoint, run one prediction, interpret the output, and learn the fastest command-line paths. Deeper topics — architecture internals, checkpoint handling, WSI pipelines — are linked at the end.

> ⚠️ **Research use only. Not for clinical or diagnostic use.** The code is PolyForm Noncommercial licensed and the weights are CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0; see [Licensing and Research Use](20-licensing-and-research-use).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L12-L44), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L13-L20)

## The Three-Step Journey

Everything in this page reduces to three operations. The first run only downloads three files from the Hugging Face repo (`config.json`, `model.safetensors`, `tokens.csv`) — the Midnight vision backbone is built offline from a bundled config and its weights come from the checkpoint, so no network access to the upstream backbone repo is needed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["pip install deepspotm"] --> B["DeepSpotM.from_pretrained<br/>(downloads config + weights + gene list)"]
    B --> C["Preprocess a 224×224 H&E tile<br/>image_processor(tile)"]
    C --> D["model(tile)<br/>→ (1, ~19k genes)"]
    D --> E["Map columns to gene symbols<br/>model.gene_names"]
```

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L251-L331), [README.md](README.md#L65-L89)

## Installation

One command installs the core package with all inference dependencies (torch, timm, peft, transformers, safetensors, huggingface_hub, and friends). Python **3.10 or newer** is required, because torch, transformers, peft and lightning all mandate it in current releases — a 3.9 install cannot resolve a working dependency set.

```bash
pip install deepspotm
```

If you plan to run the whole-slide example (or want the extras used by it), install the `wsi` extra instead. It adds `pyvips` (a libvips binding) and `anndata`:

```bash
pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"
```

To track the development branch rather than the PyPI release:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM.git
```

| Install target | Command | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Core inference | `pip install deepspotm` | Python API + `examples/predict.py` |
| Whole-slide support | `pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"` | Adds `pyvips` + `anndata` for `examples/predict_wsi.py` |
| Development branch | `pip install git+https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM.git` | Latest main, pre-release |
| Development setup | extras `test`, `dev` | pytest, ruff, build tooling |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L46-L63), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L32), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L45-L53)

## Your First Prediction

The Python API is deliberately minimal. `DeepSpotM.from_pretrained` downloads (or reads from a local directory containing) the three model files, rebuilds the architecture from the saved hyper-parameters, loads the weights, moves the model to GPU if available, sets eval mode, and returns the model together with its image transform callable:

```python
from deepspotm import DeepSpotM

model, image_processor = DeepSpotM.from_pretrained(
    "ratschlab/DeepSpotM",
    source="scgpt",   # one of evo2, orthrus, prott5, scgpt, apertus
)
```

The `source` argument selects the gene-embedding pathway the decoder uses. The released model is **multi-source** — it ships one frozen gene-embedding bank and one adapter per source — so a source *must* be named; omitting it raises a `ValueError`. The five valid choices are `evo2`, `orthrus`, `prott5`, `scgpt` (the default in every example), and `apertus`.

Now preprocess a tile and predict. `image_processor` applies the backbone's evaluation transforms (center-crop eval transforms are configured automatically), and `forward` returns a three-tuple — expression, a pooled image embedding, and attention weights (both extra outputs can be ignored for now):

```python
import torch

tile = image_processor(my_pil_tile).unsqueeze(0)   # (1, 3, 224, 224)
with torch.no_grad():
    expression, _, _ = model(tile)                 # (1, ~19k genes)
```

> [!TIP]
> At load time, `backbone_pretrained` is forced to `False`: the backbone architecture is constructed without touching the network, and every weight — backbone, LoRA adapters, gene decoder — arrives in the single `model.safetensors` file. A firewall that blocks Hugging Face but allows your environment elsewhere will still complete a local-directory load.

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L251-L331), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L318-L331), [README.md](README.md#L67-L85)

## Understanding the Output

The output vector is **log1p-CPM predicted expression** — higher means more expressed — ordered by the model's gene panel. The mapping rule is simple: output column `i` corresponds to `model.gene_names[i]`. The gene list is read once at model construction from `tokens.csv` and stored on the model, so you never need to re-parse the vocabulary yourself:

```python
preds = dict(zip(model.gene_names, expression.squeeze(0).tolist()))
```

The panel covers the ~19k genes listed in the published `tokens.csv`. Because genes are represented as queryable embeddings rather than fixed output heads, the model can even predict genes it never saw during training (zero-shot) — a property we examine in [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L83-L89), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L63-L69), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L193-L195)

## Predicting Specific Genes

Predicting the full panel for every tile is wasteful when you care about a handful of markers. `predict_genes` computes **only the requested gene queries**, which is both faster and returns a compact tensor whose columns follow your input order. It accepts a single symbol or a list, and unknown symbols raise a `KeyError` listing the offenders:

```python
vals = model.predict_genes(tile, ["EPCAM", "CD3D", "PTPRC"])   # (1, 3)
vals = model.predict_genes(tile, "EPCAM")                      # (1, 1)
```

This selection mechanism is the inference-side payoff of the gene-query design: the cross-attention decoder builds only the gene queries you ask for, skipping the rest of the panel entirely. The full mechanics are covered in [Selective Gene Prediction](16-selective-gene-prediction).

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L406-L420), [README.md](README.md#L91-L97)

## The Fastest Path: Command Line

If your goal is results rather than code, two ready-made scripts cover the two common input shapes. Both load the same Hugging Face checkpoint and share the same core flags (`--source`, `--genes`, `--device`, background filtering); run either with `--help` for the complete list.

For **pre-cut 224×224 tiles**, `examples/predict.py` scores one tile or a whole folder (recursively by default, filtering common image suffixes), prints the top-N highest-expression genes per tile, and optionally writes every prediction to a CSV. Batch size defaults to 16 tiles per forward pass:

```bash
# one tile, print the 10 highest-expression genes
python examples/predict.py tile.png

# every tile in a folder, score three markers, write a CSV
python examples/predict.py tiles/ --genes EPCAM CD3D PTPRC --output preds.csv

# different gene-embedding source, forced onto CPU
python examples/predict.py tile.png --source evo2 --device cpu
```

| Flag | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `PATH` (positional) | required | Tiles or folders of tiles; RGB, resized to 224×224 |
| `--repo` | `ratschlab/DeepSpotM` | HF repo id or local directory with the model files |
| `--source` | `scgpt` | Gene-embedding source (`evo2`/`orthrus`/`prott5`/`scgpt`/`apertus`) |
| `--genes` | full panel | Score only these symbols instead of all ~19k |
| `--top` | `10` | Highest-expression genes printed per tile (ignored with `--genes`) |
| `--output` / `-o` | none | Write all predictions to a CSV (rows = tiles, columns = genes) |
| `--batch-size` | `16` | Tiles per forward pass |
| `--skip-background` | off | Drop near-white tiles (mean pixel above `--white-mean`) |
| `--device` | auto | `cuda` if available, else `cpu` |

For **whole-slide images**, `examples/predict_wsi.py` tiles a slide on a 224-px grid at native (~20x) resolution, drops background tiles, predicts per tile, and writes a spatial AnnData `.h5ad` — the same format as the TCGA atlas, ready for scanpy/squidpy. It requires the `wsi` extra installed above:

```bash
python examples/predict_wsi.py slide.svs -o slide.h5ad
python examples/predict_wsi.py slides/ -o out/ --genes BRAF CD37 COL1A1
```

The CLI surface, performance knobs, and end-to-end examples are documented in [Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools); the slide-reading and tiling internals are covered in [Whole-Slide Image Pipeline](17-whole-slide-image-pipeline).

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L54-L110), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L15-L22), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L1-L22), [README.md](README.md#L99-L123)

## What Happens Under the Hood

It helps to see the shape of the computation you just triggered. The tile is tokenised by a LoRA-adapted pathology foundation backbone; each gene query independently attends to the patch tokens via multi-head cross-attention; and a gene router hypernetwork produces gene-specific output projections from frozen biological embeddings drawn from DNA, RNA, protein, single-cell and text foundation models:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    T["224×224 H&E tile"] --> B["LoRA-adapted vision backbone<br/>(Midnight, frozen + adapters)"]
    B --> P["Patch tokens"]
    P --> D["Cross-attention gene decoder<br/>(one query per gene)"]
    G["Frozen gene embeddings<br/>(evo2 · orthrus · prott5 · scgpt · apertus)"] --> R["Gene router hypernetwork"]
    R --> D
    D --> E["Expression vector<br/>(1, ~19k genes)"]
```

![DeepSpot-M model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

**Fig. DeepSpot-M predicts transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression from histology.** The design enables zero-shot prediction of genes at inference time because genes are queryable embeddings rather than fixed outputs.

> [!TIP]
> When `from_pretrained` returns, the model is already in eval mode with center-crop evaluation transforms active and the source pathway selected via `set_source` — you do not need to call `.eval()` or configure preprocessing yourself. The returned `image_processor` is that exact backbone transform.

You do not need any of this for basic use, but when you are ready, the components each have a dedicated page: [Pathology Vision Encoders](7-pathology-vision-encoders), [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder), and [Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L24-L42), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L60-L106)

## Project Layout at a Glance

The repository is a compact `src`-layout package. As a beginner you will touch only the first two layers — the package root and `examples/`:

```
DeepSpotM/
├── examples/                  ← runnable entry points
│   ├── predict.py             ← tile scoring CLI
│   ├── predict_wsi.py         ← whole-slide → .h5ad CLI
│   └── predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb← guided end-to-end notebook
├── src/deepspotm/             ← the installable package
│   ├── __init__.py            ← exports DeepSpotM + loading helpers
│   ├── model.py               ← DeepSpotM class, from_pretrained, predict_genes
│   ├── image_encoder.py       ← backbone construction + transforms
│   ├── modules.py             ← decoder, gene embeddings, router
│   ├── checkpoint.py          ← checkpoint/vocab loading utilities
│   ├── config.py / utils.py   ← configuration and helpers
│   └── assets/                ← bundled gene-embedding metadata
└── tests/                     ← pytest suite (test_*.py)
```

Sources: [__init__.py](src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L1-L31), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L77-L82)

## Common First-Run Issues

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ValueError: Multi-source model ... requires source=` | The released checkpoint is multi-source; the decoder refuses to guess a pathway | Pass `source="scgpt"` (or another of the five valid names) |
| `KeyError: gene(s) not in the model panel` | A gene symbol passed to `predict_genes` is not among the ~19k panel genes | Check spelling/casing against `model.gene_names` |
| Download stalls on first load | `from_pretrained` fetches three files from the Hugging Face repo on first use | Pre-download, or pass a local directory containing `config.json`, `model.safetensors`, `tokens.csv` |
| `predict.py` reports every tile filtered as background | `--skip-background` with a `--white-mean` threshold (default 220) too low for pale tiles | Lower `--white-mean` or drop `--skip-background` |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: pyvips` | Whole-slide script run without the `wsi` extra | `pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"` |
| Slow inference on CPU | Default device is `cuda` when available; large tiles fall back to CPU | Install CUDA-enabled torch, or accept smaller batches via `--batch-size` |

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L318-L327), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L393-L404), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L280-L292), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L89-L103), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L13-L14)

You now have a working model and know the two usage modes. A natural progression through this documentation:

1. **[Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools)** — master the full CLI surface, background filtering, and batch workflows before writing custom code.
2. **[TCGA-SKCM Tutorial Notebook](4-tcga-skcm-tutorial-notebook)** — a guided notebook that downloads an open-access whole-slide TCGA melanoma image, tiles it, predicts BRAF/CD37/COL1A1, and overlays predictions on the tissue end to end.
3. **[Atlas and Dataset Access](5-atlas-and-dataset-access)** — download from the published TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas (28,664 slides, 32 cancer types) to compare your predictions against.
4. **[Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview)** — when the "under the hood" sketch above leaves you curious about *why* genes-as-queries enables zero-shot prediction.


# Command-Line Prediction Tools



DeepSpot-M ships two ready-to-run prediction scripts under `examples/` that turn plain H&E histology images into predicted spatial gene expression — no Python coding required. `predict.py` scores pre-cut 224×224 image tiles, while `predict_wsi.py` takes an entire whole-slide image, tiles it for you, and writes results in a standard bioinformatics format. This page walks you through installing dependencies, choosing the right tool, understanding every command-line option, and interpreting the output.

## Two Tools, One Workflow

Both scripts are self-contained entry points built on the same underlying model. You never invoke them through a package command; you run them directly with `python examples/...` from the repository root. The key difference is the input scale: `predict.py` expects tiles already cut to 224×224 pixels, whereas `predict_wsi.py` accepts native whole-slide formats (`.svs`, `.ndpi`, `.mrxs`, and more) and performs the tiling itself on a 224-pixel grid at the slide's native (~20×) resolution.

| Aspect | `predict.py` | `predict_wsi.py` |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Single 224×224 tiles or folders of tiles | Whole-slide images (`.svs`, `.tif`, `.ndpi`, `.scn`, `.mrxs`, `.svslide`, `.bif`) |
| Tiling | You must cut tiles beforehand (any size is resized to 224×224) | Automatic, 224-px grid at native slide resolution |
| Extra dependencies | None beyond `deepspotm` | `pyvips` + `anndata` |
| Output | Ranked gene list printed to terminal, optional CSV | Spatial `.h5ad` AnnData per slide |
| Default batch size | 16 tiles | 64 tiles |
| Background filtering | Optional (`--skip-background` flag) | Always on (two-stage filter) |
| Typical use | Quick experiments on a handful of tiles | The standard "one slide in, virtual transcriptome out" workflow |

![DeepSpot-M model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

**Fig.** What happens inside each prediction: a 224×224 H&E tile is tokenized by a LoRA-adapted pathology backbone, and each gene query attends to the patch tokens through a cross-attention decoder to produce an expression value. The CLI tools are the thin user-facing wrapper around this process.

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L1-L15), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L1-L19), [README.md](README.md#L94-L121)

## Installation and Prerequisites

The core dependency installs with a single command and works on Python 3.10+:

```bash
pip install deepspotm
```

This is sufficient for `predict.py`. For `predict_wsi.py`, you additionally need `pyvips` (a fast image library backed by libvips) and `anndata` (the standard single-cell data format). There is a convenience extra:

```bash
pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"
```

If you want to run the scripts directly from a clone of this repository instead of the released package, install the development version with `pip install git+https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM.git`. Note that system-level libvips must be available for `pyvips` to import (e.g. `apt install libvips` on Debian/Ubuntu) — the script detects a missing dependency and prints a remediation hint rather than crashing with a traceback.

The relevant project layout is small: the two entry points live in `examples/`, while everything they import comes from the `src/deepspotm/` package.

```
examples/
├── predict.py          # CLI: pre-cut 224×224 tiles → terminal/CSV
└── predict_wsi.py      # CLI: whole slides → spatial .h5ad
src/deepspotm/
├── __init__.py         # exports DeepSpotM and helpers
├── model.py            # DeepSpotM class, from_pretrained(), predict_genes()
├── checkpoint.py       # checkpoint loading utilities
└── config.py           # locates the bundled gene vocabulary (tokens.csv)
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L60-L67), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L170-L180), [config.py](src/deepspotm/config.py#L5-L18), [__init__.py](src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L1-L31)

## How Both Tools Work: The Shared Pipeline

Understanding one flow explains both tools. Internally they follow the same five-stage pipeline; only the first stage (input collection) and last stage (output formatting) differ. This is deliberate — the heavy lifting (model construction, weight loading, batching, inference) is identical code in both scripts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[CLI arguments parsed] --> B[Collect input images<br/>tiles via suffix match / WSI grid]
    B --> C[Load model via<br/>DeepSpotM.from_pretrained]
    C --> D{--genes given?}
    D -->|yes| E["model.predict_genes(pixel_values, genes)<br/>only those gene queries computed"]
    D -->|no| F["model(pixel_values)<br/>full ~19k-gene panel"]
    E --> G[Batched no-grad inference<br/>results move to CPU]
    F --> G
    G --> H{Output format}
    H -->|predict.py| I[Top-N printout per tile<br/>or CSV via pandas]
    H -->|predict_wsi.py| J[Spatial AnnData .h5ad<br/>one row per tissue tile]
```

Stage C deserves a closer look because it is where both tools get the model. `DeepSpotM.from_pretrained(repo, source=...)` accepts either a Hugging Face repo id or a local directory containing three files: `config.json` (saved hyperparameters), `model.safetensors` (the weights), and `tokens.csv` (the gene vocabulary). The vision backbone is built *offline* from bundled configuration — its weights come from the checkpoint, so no network access to the upstream backbone repository is needed. The call returns a tuple: the model already in eval mode with center-crop evaluation transforms, and an `image_processor` callable that turns PIL images into the tensor format the model expects.

> [!TIP]
> The `--source` flag selects which gene-embedding pathway the decoder uses (`evo2`, `orthrus`, `prott5`, `scgpt`, `apertus`). The published model is multi-source, so a source must always be active before inference — both CLIs default to `scgpt`, and if you build the model programmatically without specifying one, `from_pretrained` raises an error listing the available choices rather than guessing.

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L148-L166), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L200-L202), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L251-L331), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L318-L327)

## Predicting Pre-Cut Tiles with predict.py

`predict.py` is the fastest way to sanity-check the model. Point it at a single tile or a whole folder — folders are searched recursively by default, and any file with an image suffix (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.tif`, `.tiff`, `.bmp`, `.webp`) is picked up and deduplicated.

```bash
# one tile, print the 10 highest-expression genes
python examples/predict.py tile.png

# every tile in a folder, score three marker genes, write a CSV
python examples/predict.py tiles/ --genes EPCAM CD3D PTPRC --output preds.csv

# a different gene-embedding source, forced onto CPU
python examples/predict.py tile.png --source evo2 --device cpu
```

The step-by-step execution within the script looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Expand paths to<br/>sorted image list] --> T{--skip-background?}
    T -->|yes| U[Drop tiles whose<br/>mean pixel > white-mean]
    T -->|no| V[Keep all tiles]
    U --> W[Accumulate batch of<br/>batch-size preprocessed tiles]
    V --> W
    W --> X[torch.no_grad forward<br/>predict_genes or full panel]
    X --> Y[Concatenate CPU results]
    Y --> Z{--output?}
    Z -->|yes| AA[Write CSV<br/>rows=tiles, cols=genes]
    Z -->|no| AB[Print ranked genes per tile]
```

Two behaviors matter for beginners. First, **without `--genes`** the script predicts the full panel and prints the `--top` highest-expression genes per tile, sorted descending — useful for exploring what a tile "looks like" molecularly. Second, **with `--genes`** the script calls `model.predict_genes()`, which maps your gene symbols to column indices and computes only those gene queries in the decoder. This is genuinely faster, not just cosmetic filtering: the cross-attention decoder builds fewer gene queries, so less compute happens per tile.

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L8-L13), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L101-L146), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L180-L195), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L406-L420)

## Predicting Whole Slides with predict_wsi.py

This is the tool most users start from — the README's own recommendation. Give it a slide file or a folder of slides, and it produces one `.h5ad` per slide:

```bash
# one slide -> one .h5ad (full ~19k-gene panel)
python examples/predict_wsi.py slide.svs -o slide.h5ad

# a folder of slides -> one .h5ad each in out/, scoring three marker genes
python examples/predict_wsi.py slides/ -o out/ --genes BRAF CD37 COL1A1
```

The output behavior is filename-driven: if you pass exactly one slide and the `-o` argument ends in `.h5ad`, that exact filename is used; in any other case, `-o` is treated as a directory and each slide gets `<slide-name>.h5ad` inside it.

Whole-slide prediction introduces one genuinely clever piece of engineering: a **two-stage background filter**. Whole slides are mostly empty glass, and naively reading every 224×224 tile at full resolution would be slow. Instead, the script first builds a tiny one-pixel-per-tile thumbnail of the entire slide and flags candidate tissue tiles cheaply from that thumbnail; only flagged candidates are then cropped at full resolution and re-checked against the exact `--white-mean` threshold before being kept.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Open slide with pyvips<br/>access=random] --> B[Build thumbnail,<br/>one pixel per grid cell]
    B --> C[Candidate tissue tiles:<br/>thumbnail mean <= white_mean + 10]
    C --> D[Crop each candidate<br/>at full 224px resolution]
    D --> E{exact mean ><br/>white_mean?}
    E -->|yes| F[Discard: background glass]
    E -->|no| G[Queue tile with x,y coordinates]
    G --> H[Batched prediction,<br/>default 64 tiles per pass]
    H --> I[to_anndata: expression +<br/>tile-center coordinates]
    I --> J[Write .h5ad]
```

> [!TIP]
> The thumbnail filter intentionally uses a *looser* threshold (`white_mean + 10`) than the exact check, so no tissue tile is ever rejected in the cheap first pass — the strict `--white-mean` decision only happens at full resolution. If your slide comes back with zero tiles, the message tells you to *raise* `--white-mean` (e.g. to 230–240), because your tissue is darker than the default 220 cutoff allows.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L36-L64), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L170-L195), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L216-L220), [README.md](README.md#L94-L106)

## Shared Options Reference

Every option below works identically in both scripts (only the defaults for `--batch-size` differ, and `--top`/`--skip-background`/`--tile` are tool-specific). Run either script with `--help` for the inline reference including worked examples.

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `inputs` (positional) | required | One or more files/folders; folders are searched recursively by default |
| `--repo` | `ratschlab/DeepSpotM` | Hugging Face repo id **or** a local directory with `config.json` + `model.safetensors` + `tokens.csv` |
| `--source` | `scgpt` | Gene-embedding pathway: one of `evo2`, `orthrus`, `prott5`, `scgpt`, `apertus` |
| `--genes` | full panel | Score only these gene symbols; also faster (fewer decoder queries) |
| `--output` / `-o` | print to terminal (predict.py) / `.` (predict_wsi.py) | CSV file for tiles; `.h5ad` file or directory for slides |
| `--batch-size` | 16 / 64 | Tiles per forward pass — raise on GPUs with ample memory |
| `--white-mean` | `220.0` | Mean-pixel value above which a tile counts as background |
| `--skip-background` | off (predict.py only) | Apply the background filter to tile folders |
| `--tile` | `224` | Grid size in pixels (predict_wsi.py only) |
| `--top` | `10` | How many top genes to print per tile (predict.py only, ignored with `--genes`) |
| `--no-recursive` | off | Don't descend into sub-folders |
| `--device` | `cuda` if available, else `cpu` | Force `cuda` or `cpu` |

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L41-L99), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L126-L168)

## Understanding the Output

All predicted values are in **log1p-CPM** units — the log of counts-per-million plus one, the same scale used by the published TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas. Higher values mean more expressed; the scale is comparable across tiles and directly compatible with downstream scanpy/squidpy analyses.

The mapping from output columns to gene names is strictly ordered. When you omit `--genes`, output column `i` corresponds to `model.gene_names[i]` — the ~19k-gene panel loaded from `tokens.csv`. When you pass `--genes EPCAM CD3D PTPRC`, the output columns follow exactly the order you typed. The `.h5ad` output encodes everything a spatial analysis needs: `X` holds the expression matrix, `adata.obsm["spatial"]` holds tile-center pixel coordinates in the standard squidpy/scanpy convention, `obs` rows are named `<slide>_<x>_<y>`, and `adata.uns["deepspotm"]` records provenance (slide name, tile size, embedding source, and the expression unit).

| Consumer | Format | Columns / fields |
|---|---|---|
| Terminal (predict.py, no `--genes`) | Ranked list | Top-N gene names + values per tile |
| Terminal (predict.py, with `--genes`) | Inline scores | `gene=value` pairs in your given order |
| CSV (predict.py, `--output`) | pandas DataFrame | rows = tile filenames, columns = genes, index named `tile` |
| AnnData (predict_wsi.py) | `.h5ad` | `X` (log1p-CPM), `obsm["spatial"]`, `obs`, `var`, `uns["deepspotm"]` |

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L182-L203), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L106-L124), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L67-L70), [README.md](README.md#L85-L92)

## Troubleshooting and Exit Codes

Both scripts are designed to fail loudly but gracefully: they catch expected problems, print a one-line `error:` message to stderr, and return exit code 1 (0 on success). This makes them safe to embed in pipelines. The most common beginner pitfalls are already anticipated by the scripts' own error messages:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `error: unknown gene symbol(s): ...` | A `--genes` symbol isn't in the model's panel; validated against `tokens.csv` | Check spelling; list valid names via `model.gene_names` |
| `error: every tile was filtered as background` (predict.py) | `--white-mean` too low for pale scans, or folder genuinely empty | Lower the threshold or drop `--skip-background` |
| `skipped: no tissue tiles found` (predict_wsi.py) | Threshold rejects all tiles | *Raise* `--white-mean` (default 220) so darker tissue passes |
| `ImportError: pyvips / anndata` (predict_wsi.py) | WSI extras not installed | `pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"` and ensure libvips is on the system |
| No image files found | Extension not in the supported set, or `--no-recursive` hid files in sub-folders | Check suffixes; re-enable recursion |

Note the per-slide behavior of `predict_wsi.py`: an unknown gene or an all-background slide skips *that* slide, sets the final exit code to 1, and continues with the remaining slides — a folder of 50 slides with one bad file still produces 49 outputs.

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L151-L155), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L172-L179), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L170-L195), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L204-L226), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L393-L404)

## Where to Go Next

Once your first predictions run, the natural progression is:

- **See it end-to-end with visuals** — the [TCGA-SKCM Tutorial Notebook](4-tcga-skcm-tutorial-notebook) downloads a real whole-slide image, runs the same pipeline, and overlays predicted gene expression on the tissue.
- **Understand what the model is doing** — the [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview) explains the vision encoder and cross-attention decoder behind every prediction you just made, with the [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder) covering why `--genes` is faster.
- **Go deeper on the machinery you just used** — [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading) dissects `from_pretrained`, [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping) explains the `gene_names` column ordering, and [Selective Gene Prediction](16-selective-gene-prediction) covers the `predict_genes` path in detail.
- **Master the WSI pipeline** — [Whole-Slide Image Pipeline](17-whole-slide-image-pipeline) expands on the tiling and background filtering you saw here.

If you haven't installed the package yet, start with [Quick Start](2-quick-start).


# TCGA-SKCM Tutorial Notebook



This page documents `examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb`, the repository's hands-on walkthrough for running **DeepSpot-M end to end on a real whole-slide H&E image**. In five notebook cells you download an open-access melanoma slide from the TCGA portal, tile it into model-sized patches, predict three marker genes per tile in zero-shot mode, and render atlas-style spatial expression maps — exactly the workflow behind the published TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L4-L46)

## What the Notebook Demonstrates

The tutorial operates on one open-access **TCGA-SKCM (skin cutaneous melanoma)** slide, `TCGA-D9-A3Z3-06Z-00-DX1`, and predicts three marker genes chosen to reveal the three tissue compartments a pathologist looks for:

| Gene | Marks |
|------|-------|
| BRAF | melanoma driver oncogene, tumour |
| CD37 | lymphocyte marker, tumour-infiltrating immune cells |
| COL1A1 | collagen gene, stroma |

The slide gives a concrete sense of scale: **99,960 × 65,991 pixels**, which becomes a 446 × 294 tile grid. A fast thumbnail pass nominates 45,751 candidate tissue tiles; the exact background filter keeps 36,392, and only those are scored by the model. One important caveat the notebook states up front: the published melanoma atlas used a model *finetuned* on melanoma spatial transcriptomics, while this tutorial uses the **base released model in zero-shot mode**, so the resulting maps are illustrative and softer than the atlas figures.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L4-L46)

Under the hood, DeepSpot-M tokenises each 224×224 H&E tile with a LoRA-adapted pathology vision foundation model, and each gene queries the patch tokens through a cross-attention gene decoder. Because genes are *queryable embeddings* rather than fixed output heads, one model covers the transcriptome — including genes it never saw during training.

![DeepSpotM model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

The complete tutorial pipeline is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Install deepspotm[wsi] + matplotlib"] --> B["Log in to Hugging Face Hub (gated weights)"]
    B --> C["Download ~1 GB SVS from GDC by UUID"]
    C --> D{"MD5 checksum matches?"}
    D -- "no" --> E["Delete file and re-download"]
    D -- "yes" --> F["Open slide lazily with pyvips, access=random"]
    F --> G["Thumbnail pass: 1 pixel per tile,<br/>mean <= 230 -> candidate grid"]
    G --> H["Load DeepSpotM.from_pretrained<br/>source=scgpt -> (model, image_processor)"]
    H --> I["Crop each candidate 224x224 tile"]
    I --> J{"Exact filter:<br/>tile mean <= 220?"}
    J -- "background" --> I
    J -- "tissue" --> K["image_processor -> batch of 128"]
    K --> L["model.predict_genes(px, GENES)"]
    L --> M["Collect coords + log1p-CPM values<br/>(36,392 x 3)"]
    M --> N["Scatter-overlay on 2000-px H&E overview"]
```

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L4-L46), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L407-L421)

## Prerequisites and Setup

The notebook's first markdown cell gives the full environment contract: install `pip install "deepspotm[wsi]" matplotlib`, where the `wsi` extra pulls in the whole-slide imaging stack defined in the package metadata. `pyvips` additionally needs the **system** `libvips` library built with OpenSlide support, and a **GPU is recommended** because the model processes tens of thousands of tiles.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L4-L46), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L58-L63)

| Package | Constraint | Role in this tutorial |
|---------|------------|----------------------|
| pyvips | >=2.2 | Lazy, random-access reading of the pyramidal `.svs` slide |
| anndata | >=0.10 | AnnData I/O for the broader WSI pipeline (shipped with the extra) |
| matplotlib | unpinned | Rendering the four-panel expression maps |

The model weights are **gated on the Hugging Face Hub**, so you must request access to `ratschlab/DeepSpotM` and authenticate once with `huggingface-cli login` before `from_pretrained` can download anything.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L4-L46), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L58-L63)

> [!TIP]
> Import order matters: the notebook imports `pyvips` **before** `torch` in its first code cell, because libvips/glib initialisation can fail if torch loads first. Preserve this ordering if you refactor the cells.

The setup cell then pins the tutorial's tunable constants in one place, making the experiment easy to adapt:

| Constant | Value | Purpose |
|----------|-------|---------|
| `GENES` | `["BRAF", "CD37", "COL1A1"]` | Marker genes scored per tile |
| `TILE` | `224` | Model input tile size in pixels |
| `WHITE_MEAN` | `220` | Exact background threshold (mean pixel value) |
| `BATCH` | `128` | Tiles per forward pass |
| `DEVICE` | `cuda` if available, else `cpu` | Compute device, printed at startup |

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L63-L77)

## Step 1 — Download and Verify the Slide

The slide is fetched from the **GDC Data Portal** by file UUID without any authentication token, saved as `TCGA-D9-A3Z3-06Z-00-DX1.svs`, and skipped if already present so the cell is idempotent. Integrity is enforced via a hard-coded MD5 (`2fae5ac0b57505fb704efaa0d950846b`). Notably, the checksum is computed by hashing the file in **8 MB chunks** rather than loading the whole ~1 GB slide into memory — the notebook explicitly notes that reading it fully into RAM would spike memory more than the model itself uses. This is a pattern worth copying for any large-file verification step.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L105-L123)

## Step 2 — Locate Tissue Tiles

An `.svs` file is a **pyramidal** whole-slide image, so the notebook opens it lazily with `pyvips.Image.new_from_file(..., access="random")` and never materialises the full resolution array. Tissue detection is deliberately two-stage:

1. **Thumbnail pass (cheap, approximate).** A thumbnail with one pixel per tile is resized to the exact grid shape; tiles whose thumbnail mean is `<= WHITE_MEAN + 10` become candidates. The +10 margin keeps the pass loose.
2. **Exact pass (per tile).** Each candidate tile is cropped at full resolution via a small `read_tile(x, y)` helper, and the precise `mean > 220` filter is applied only then.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L131-L175)

> [!TIP]
> The two-stage filter exists to avoid paying full-resolution crop costs for obvious background: 45,751 candidates enter the loop but only 36,392 survive the exact check. If you retune `WHITE_MEAN`, remember the thumbnail pass uses `WHITE_MEAN + 10`, so the two thresholds drift together.

## Step 3 — Load the Pretrained Model

A single call loads everything the tutorial needs:

```python
model, image_processor = DeepSpotM.from_pretrained("ratschlab/DeepSpotM", source="scgpt")
model = model.to(DEVICE).eval()
assert all(g in set(model.gene_names) for g in GENES)
```

The `source="scgpt"` argument selects the gene-embedding pathway used by the decoder (`scgpt` is the package default, alongside `evo2`, `orthrus`, `prott5`, `apertus`). Internally, `from_pretrained` fetches three files from the Hub — `config.json` (hyper-parameters including `bio_dims`), `model.safetensors` (vision backbone + LoRA adapters + gene decoder), and `tokens.csv` (the gene vocabulary) — rebuilds the architecture offline (the upstream backbone weights come from the checkpoint, not from the backbone's own repo), loads the weights with validation, activates the chosen source, and switches the image transforms to **center-crop eval transforms at 224 px** before returning the `(model, image_processor)` pair.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["from_pretrained(repo, source)"] --> B{"Local dir or<br/>HF repo id?"}
    B -- "repo id" --> C["hf_hub_download:<br/>config.json, model.safetensors, tokens.csv"]
    B -- "local dir" --> D["Read the same three files"]
    C --> E["Rebuild model from config.json<br/>backbone built offline"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Load safetensors<br/>strict=False + validation"]
    F --> G["set_source: one active<br/>gene-embedding pathway"]
    G --> H["eval() + center-crop<br/>224 px transforms"]
    H --> I["Returns (model, image_processor)"]
```

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L202-L204), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L255-L320), [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L53-L58)

The final `assert` is the notebook's safety net: `model.gene_names` is the **ordered vocabulary** where output column *i* of the decoder corresponds to `gene_names[i]`, and the assertion fails fast if any of the three marker genes is absent from the panel before 36k tiles are wasted on a doomed run.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L202-L204), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L83-L90)

## Step 4 — Predict Gene Expression Tile by Tile

The prediction loop streams tiles through the model in batches of 128 and never holds the whole slide in memory. For each kept tile, the PIL image is passed through `image_processor` (the backbone's 224 px eval transform), stacked into a `(B, 3, 224, 224)` tensor, moved to the GPU, and scored with:

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model.predict_genes(px, GENES).float().cpu().numpy()
```

The helper accumulates `(x, y)` coordinates alongside expression rows in lockstep, so after the loop `coords` and the concatenated `(36392, 3)` expression matrix are index-aligned — this alignment is exactly what the overlay step depends on. Values live in **log1p-CPM space**: higher means more expressed.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L202-L231)

The reason this is affordable is `predict_genes` itself. It maps gene symbols to decoder indices via `genes_to_indices` (raising a `KeyError` that lists any unknown symbols), then runs the cross-attention decoder over **only those gene queries** — asking for 3 genes is dramatically cheaper than the full panel of roughly 19k. The method also carries a built-in `@torch.no_grad()` decorator, so prediction calls are gradient-free even if you forget the context manager:

| Aspect | Full-panel forward | Selective `predict_genes` |
|--------|--------------------|---------------------------|
| Call | `out, _, _ = model(pixel_values)` | `out = model.predict_genes(pixel_values, GENES)` |
| Genes computed | Entire panel (~19k gene queries) | Only the requested gene queries |
| Output shape | `(B, n_genes)` | `(B, len(GENES))`, columns in `GENES` order |
| Unknown symbol handling | Silent index errors possible | `KeyError` naming the offending symbols |
| Gradient guard | Caller must wrap `torch.no_grad()` | Built-in `@torch.no_grad()` |
| Typical use | Top-N expression ranking, CSV dumps | Targeted marker panels, WSI sweeps |

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L407-L421), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L390-L405), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L98-L140)

## Step 5 — Render the Spatial Expression Maps

The final cell produces the figure that motivates the whole tutorial. A 2000-pixel overview thumbnail of the slide provides the H&E backdrop; each scored tile is drawn at its **centre** (top-left coordinate + `TILE / 2`, scaled by the thumbnail factors `sx, sy`) with `matplotlib` scatter coloured by predicted expression (`cmap="viridis"`). The result is a four-panel figure — raw H&E plus one map per gene — titled "DeepSpot-M predicted expression, TCGA-D9-A3Z3 (SKCM)". The expected biology: **BRAF** lights up the tumour, **CD37** the immune infiltrate, and **COL1A1** the stroma, reproducing the three-compartment picture shown in the atlas.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L260-L279)

## Notebook vs. Command-Line Prediction

The repository ships a second entry point, `examples/predict.py`, which shares the same model APIs but targets a different workflow. Use this table to pick the right tool:

| Dimension | `predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb` (this tutorial) | `predict.py` (CLI) |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------|---------------------|
| Input | One whole-slide `.svs`, downloaded from GDC | Tile images or folders (PNG/JPG/TIFF/BMP/WEBP) |
| Scope | End-to-end: download → tile → predict → visualise | Prediction only, on images you already have |
| Dependencies | `deepspotm[wsi]` (pyvips) + matplotlib | Base install (Pillow suffices) |
| Gene selection | `GENES` list via `predict_genes` | `--genes`, or full panel with top-N printing |
| Background filter | Thumbnail pass + exact per-tile mean filter | Opt-in `--skip-background` with `--white-mean` |
| Batch size | 128 | 16 by default (`--batch-size`) |
| Output | Matplotlib spatial maps in-notebook | Stdout ranking and/or CSV via `--output` |
| Device | Auto `cuda`/`cpu` | `--device` override supported |

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L1-L29), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L31-L95)

## Troubleshooting

The notebook and the CLI both fail loudly at well-defined points. Match your symptom to the fix:

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|---------|------------|-----|
| `AssertionError: checksum mismatch: ...` | Interrupted or corrupted ~1 GB download | Delete the `.svs` and re-run the download cell |
| `KeyError: N gene(s) not in the model panel` | Symbol absent from `tokens.csv` vocabulary | Check spelling; verify against `model.gene_names` first |
| `kept tissue tiles: 0` | Threshold too strict for the slide region | Raise `WHITE_MEAN` or inspect the thumbnail pass output |
| 401/403 errors from Hugging Face | Gated weights, not authenticated | Request access to the model repo, then `huggingface-cli login` |
| libvips/OpenSlide load failure | System library missing or built without OpenSlide | Install libvips with OpenSlide support (required by the `wsi` extra) |
| GLib initialisation crash at import | `torch` imported before `pyvips` | Keep the notebook's import order: pyvips first |

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L105-L123), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L390-L405), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L58-L63)

A logical progression: run [Quick Start](2-quick-start) first if you haven't installed the package, then compare the tile-level workflow with [Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools). After finishing here, [Atlas and Dataset Access](5-atlas-and-dataset-access) explains where the finetuned atlas predictions (and the data behind them) live. # Atlas and Dataset Access



DeepSpot-M ships not only a model but also the transcriptome-scale predictions it produced. This page covers the two released prediction resources — the **TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas** and the **HEST Xenium virtual single-cell profiles** — their gated access workflow on the Hugging Face Hub, the on-disk AnnData schema, the provenance of the predictions, and how to generate atlas-compatible data from your own slides. Everything here is data access and provenance; model internals are deferred to [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview).

## The Released Datasets at a Glance

The project distributes two prediction resources, both hosted as gated Hugging Face datasets. The TCGA atlas is the pan-cancer bulk resource, while the HEST release extends the same prediction machinery to single-cell-resolution Xenium assays on 59 public HEST-1K samples.

| Property | TCGA Virtual Atlas | HEST Xenium Profiles |
|---|---|---|
| Hub repo id | `ratschlab/TCGA_virtual_spatial_transcriptomics_atlas` | `ratschlab/HEST_Xenium_virtual_spatial_transcriptomics` |
| Scale | 28,664 whole-slide images, 32 cancer types | 59 HEST-1K samples |
| Spots | 295.3 million spots from 10,865 patients | Single-cell resolution profiles |
| Payload | Predicted log1p-CPM expression over the full transcriptome per spot | Virtual single-cell Xenium profiles |
| Layout | `data/<cancer>/<FF\|FFPE>/<slide_id>.h5ad.gz` + `metadata.csv` | Per-sample profiles (see dataset card) |
| Access | Gated — request access + HF login | Hosted on the Hub alongside the atlas |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L137-L171), [README.md](README.md#L173-L178)

## End-to-End Data Flow

The atlas is the result of applying DeepSpot-M — with cancer-specific finetuning — to open-access TCGA slides sourced from the GDC Data Portal, then publishing the per-spot predictions as compressed AnnData files on a gated Hub dataset. Your access path never touches the model: you authenticate once, then stream selected subsets with `snapshot_download` into scanpy/squidpy-ready files. A second path exists for producing identically formatted data from your own slides via the WSI example script.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph upstream["Upstream (authors' pipeline)"]
        GDC["TCGA H&E WSIs<br/>(GDC Data Portal, open access)"]
        MODEL["DeepSpot-M<br/>cancer-specific finetuned"]
    end
    subgraph hub["Hugging Face Hub — gated"]
        TCGA["TCGA atlas<br/>28,664 slides / 32 cancers"]
        HEST["HEST Xenium profiles<br/>59 samples"]
        META["metadata.csv"]
    end
    subgraph local["Your machine"]
        AUTH["HF token + access grant"]
        SD["snapshot_download<br/>allow_patterns"]
        ANALYSIS["scanpy / squidpy"]
    end
    GDC --> MODEL --> TCGA
    TCGA --> HEST
    TCGA --> META
    AUTH --> SD
    TCGA --> SD
    HEST --> SD
    SD --> ANALYSIS
```

The HEST branch in the diagram reflects that the Xenium release derives from the same prediction machinery rather than being a subset of the TCGA files — it is a separate Hub repo you download independently.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L137-L171), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L4-L14)

## Gated Access: Authentication and Selective Download

The TCGA atlas is **gated**: before any download works you must request access on the dataset page, create an HF token, and authenticate. The README's canonical access pattern uses `huggingface_hub`'s `login` plus `snapshot_download` with `allow_patterns` to fetch only what you need — the full atlas is explicitly flagged as large, so selective patterns are the recommended default.

```python
from huggingface_hub import login, snapshot_download
login(token="YOUR_HF_TOKEN")

repo = "ratschlab/TCGA_virtual_spatial_transcriptomics_atlas"
snapshot_download(repo, repo_type="dataset", local_dir="TCGA_data",
                  allow_patterns="data/TCGA_SKCM/*")
```

The repository path structure makes pattern-based subsetting precise:

| Strategy | `allow_patterns` | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| One cancer cohort | `data/TCGA_SKCM/*` | All melanoma slides, both FF and FFPE |
| One preservation type, all cancers | `data/*/FFPE/*` | Every FFPE slide across all 32 cancer types |
| Fresh-frozen only | `data/*/FF/*` | Every fresh-frozen slide |
| Full atlas | *(no pattern)* | Everything — described as "large" |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L149-L167)

## On-Disk Schema of the Atlas

Each sample is a **gzip-compressed AnnData** file following the pattern `data/<cancer>/<FF|FFPE>/<slide_id>.h5ad.gz`. The expression matrix `X` holds predicted **log1p-CPM** values over the full transcriptome, and a single top-level `metadata.csv` indexes every sample with its cancer type, slide type, and spot count. This mirrors the ~19k-gene panel the model emits, ordered by `model.gene_names` (see [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping)).

| Schema element | Location | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Per-slide predictions | `data/<cancer>/<FF\|FFPE>/<slide_id>.h5ad.gz` | Compressed AnnData, one entry per spot |
| Expression matrix | `X` in each `.h5ad.gz` | Predicted log1p-CPM, full transcriptome (~19k genes) |
| Cohort index | `metadata.csv` | Cancer type, slide type (FF/FFPE), spot count per sample |
| Overlay example | Dataset card | Loading a sample and overlaying predicted genes on the H&E |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L144-L149), [README.md](README.md#L169-L171)

> [!TIP]
> The `metadata.csv` index is your query layer for cohort construction — filter it locally by cancer type and slide type first, then translate the survivors into precise `allow_patterns` so you never download slides you will discard.

## Provenance: Finetuned Atlas vs Zero-Shot Tutorial

A critical caveat when comparing atlas files against your own predictions: the published atlas predictions for the **trained cancer types** (melanoma among them) were produced with **cancer-specific finetuned models**, while the tutorial notebook uses the base released model in **zero-shot mode** — so tutorial-derived maps look softer than the corresponding atlas. The tutorial deliberately reproduces the atlas example figure (BRAF tumour / CD37 immune infiltrate / COL1A1 stroma on slide `TCGA-D9-A3Z3-06Z-00-DX1`) to make this difference directly visible.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L125-L135), [examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L20-L46)

## Fetching Upstream Slides from the GDC

When you want to regenerate or extend atlas-style predictions, the raw slides come from the **GDC Data Portal**, where the example slide is open-access and fetchable **by file UUID without a token**. The tutorial pairs each UUID with an MD5 checksum, hashing in 8 MB chunks so verifying a ~1 GB slide never spikes memory. For scale orientation: this slide is 99,960 × 65,991 px, yielding 45,751 candidate tiles from the thumbnail pass, of which 36,392 survive the exact background filter.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["GDC Data Portal<br/>fetch by file UUID (no token)"] --> B["MD5 verification<br/>8 MB chunked hashing"]
    B --> C["Thumbnail pass<br/>45,751 candidate tissue tiles"]
    C --> D["Exact background filter<br/>mean pixel ≤ 220 → 36,392 tiles"]
    D --> E["predict_genes<br/>BRAF, CD37, COL1A1, batch 128"]
    E --> F["Overlay predictions on H&E"]
```

Sources: [examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L84-L123), [examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L29-L40)

## Generating Atlas-Compatible Data Yourself

The cleanest way to produce data in the atlas format is [`examples/predict_wsi.py`](examples/predict_wsi.py), which reads a slide, tiles it on a 224-px grid at native (~20x) resolution, drops background, predicts per tile, and writes a spatial AnnData — **the same format as the TCGA atlas**, ready for scanpy/squidpy. The provenance you would otherwise have to reconstruct is embedded directly in the output file.

| AnnData field | Written by `to_anndata` | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `X` | Predicted expression, float32 | log1p-CPM, full ~19k panel or `--genes` subset |
| `obs` | `x`, `y` columns | Tile origin pixel coordinates |
| `var` | Gene symbols | Panel ordered as `model.gene_names` |
| `obsm["spatial"]` | Tile centers | squidpy/scanpy spatial convention |
| `uns["deepspotm"]` | `slide`, `tile_px`, `source`, `expression="log1p-CPM"` | Full provenance record |

This symmetry is what makes the tutorial's overlay workflow applicable verbatim to atlas files or to your own outputs: both are ordinary AnnData with `obsm["spatial"]` coordinates.

Sources: [examples/predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L1-L18), [examples/predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L128-L146), [README.md](README.md#L99-L105)

## Licensing Constraints for Dataset Use

The project uses a **split license**: code under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, model weights under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0. Because the atlas content consists of model outputs from those weights, the NonCommercial and ShareAlike obligations extend to what you build from it: attribution with citation of the paper, no commercial use of weights or their outputs, and ShareAlike terms if you transform or build upon them. The released work is explicitly research use only, not for clinical or diagnostic use; the backbone and gene-embedding sources are separately MIT or Apache-2.0 (see [Licensing and Research Use](20-licensing-and-research-use)).

Sources: [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L1-L20), [README.md](README.md#L180-L189)

## Where This Fits in the Repository

The files relevant to dataset access concentrate in a few places — the two example scripts and notebook are the reference implementations for both consuming and producing atlas-format data:

```
examples/
├── predict_wsi.py            # slide → atlas-format .h5ad (producer)
├── predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb   # GDC slide → overlay figure (consumer workflow)
└── predict.py                # pre-cut 224x224 tiles → CSV / top genes

```

![DeepSpot-M model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

The figure above summarizes the model whose predictions populate the atlas — the cross-attention gene decoder and gene router hypernetwork shown here are detailed in [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder) and [Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork).

# Architecture Overview



DeepSpot-M is a multimodal foundation model that maps a 224×224 H&E histology tile to transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression. This page gives you the system-level view: how the three architectural stages (vision encoding → cross-attention decoding → hypernetwork projection) compose into a single forward pass, which module owns which responsibility, and the design principles that make every component an ablation switch. Component internals (per-encoder details, LoRA mechanics, decoder math) live in the dedicated Deep Dive pages; this page stops at the boundaries between them.

## The Model in One Data Flow

The published model figure captures the complete forward path: a LoRA-adapted pathology backbone tokenizes the tile into spatial patch embeddings, gene queries attend to those patches through cross-attention, and a hypernetwork converts refined queries into per-gene expression values. Because genes are represented as *queryable embeddings* rather than fixed output columns, the same network predicts the full ~19k-gene panel and genes it never saw during training (zero-shot).

![DeepSpot-M model overview](https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM/blob/main/assets/model_overview.png?raw=true)

Fig. DeepSpot-M predicts transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression from histology [README](README.md#L29-L44)

The code-level data flow follows the same shape. Patch tokens are extracted from the backbone (bypassing CLS pooling), projected into a shared 256-d space to form the cross-attention keys/values, gene queries derived from biological embeddings form the queries, two cross-attention layers refine them, and a per-gene hypernetwork produces the final `(B, G)` expression vector:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    TILE["H&E tile<br/>(B, 3, 224, 224)"] --> ENC

    subgraph VISION["Stage 1 · Vision backbone"]
        ENC["ImageEncoder<br/>(Midnight ViT by default)"]
        LORA["PEFT LoRA adapters<br/>r=8, alpha=16"] -.->|"adapts"| ENC
    end

    ENC -->|"patch tokens (B, N, D_patch)"| PROJ

    subgraph DECODE["Stage 2 · Cross-attention gene decoder"]
        PROJ["patch_proj: Linear(D_patch → 256)<br/>= keys / values"]
        QA["Gene queries (B, G, 256)<br/>bio embedding → adapter → + modality one-hot"]
        CA["CrossAttentionLayer × 2<br/>8 heads, FFN ×4, pre-norm residuals"]
    end

    PROJ -->|"K/V (B, N, 256)"| CA
    QA --> CA

    CA -->|"refined queries (B, G, 256)"| ROUTE

    subgraph ROUTE["Stage 3 · Gene router hypernetwork"]
        ROUTER["weight_net / bias_net<br/>bio_dim → 256-d projection + bias"]
    end

    ROUTER --> OUT["expression (B, G)<br/>G ≈ 19k genes, column i = gene_names[i]"]
```

The three stages map one-to-one onto the library's top-level components: `ImageEncoder` (with its PEFT LoRA wrapper), `CrossAttentionGeneDecoder`, and `GeneRouter`, all orchestrated by the `DeepSpotM` LightningModule.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L44), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L369-L384), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L713-L790)

## Module Map: Who Owns What

The repository is deliberately flat — eight source files under `src/deepspotm/`, each with a single architectural concern. Reading the file list is nearly reading the architecture:

```
src/deepspotm/
├── model.py           # DeepSpotM: orchestration, forward, source dispatch, loading
├── image_encoder.py   # ImageEncoder contract + 7-backbone registry
├── modules.py         # decoder, router, multi-source embeddings, vocabulary
├── checkpoint.py      # state-dict filtering & inference-time reconstruction
├── config.py          # bundled asset paths (tokens.csv, midnight_config.json)
├── utils.py           # image transforms (get_eval_transforms, normalize params)
└── assets/            # gene-embedding priors, tokens.csv, backbone configs
```

| Layer | Class(es) | File | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| Orchestration | `DeepSpotM` | [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L11-L37) | Wires backbone + decoder; exposes `forward`, `predict_genes`, `set_source`, `from_pretrained` |
| Vision | `ImageEncoder` + 7 concrete encoders | [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L24-L81) | Patch-token extraction behind a uniform contract |
| Gene queries | `MultiSourceGeneEmbedding` | [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L148-L181) | Per-source bio embedding + adapter + modality encoding, runtime source dispatch |
| Decoding | `CrossAttentionGeneDecoder`, `CrossAttentionLayer` | [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L473-L520) | Gene-queries-attend-to-patches refinement |
| Output head | `GeneRouter` (hypernetwork) | [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L110-L145) | Per-gene projection weights → expression |
| Vocabulary | `StructureExpression` | [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L17-L39) | Ordered gene panel from `tokens.csv`; label mapping |
| Persistence | `load_for_prediction`, state-dict filters | [checkpoint.py](src/deepspotm/checkpoint.py#L84-L131) | Cross-vocab and multi-source checkpoint reconstruction |

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L11-L37), [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L24-L81), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L473-L520), [checkpoint.py](src/deepspotm/checkpoint.py#L84-L131)

## The Vision Stage: A Registry of Interchangeable Backbones

Every vision backbone in the codebase inherits from one abstract `ImageEncoder` class that fixes the contract the rest of the architecture depends on. The contract has four members: `forward_patch_tokens()` returns spatial tokens `(B, N, D)` with CLS/register prefixes stripped (with generic handling for timm and HuggingFace model families), the `patch_dim` property reports per-token dimensionality (which the decoder consumes to size its projection), `LORA_TARGET_MODULES` declares which linear layers LoRA should attach to, and `NORM_MEAN`/`NORM_STD` drive the paired image transforms.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L24-L81)

Concrete backbones are registered in a name → class dict and built through a `build_encoder(name)` factory, so swapping the vision stage is a single string change (`encoder_model="MidnightEncoder"`). The shipped registry spans seven pathology-relevant encoders:

| Registry key | Source model | Patch dim | Pooled hidden dim | Default? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `MidnightEncoder` | kaiko-ai/midnight (HF AutoModel) | 1536 | 3072 (CLS + mean patch) | ✅ default |
| `UNI1Encoder` | MahmoodLab/UNI (ViT-L/16) | 1024 | 1024 (CLS) | — |
| `UNI2Encoder` | MahmoodLab/UNI2-h (ViT-G/14 + SwiGLU) | 1536 | 1536 (CLS) | — |
| `H0Encoder` / `H1Encoder` | H-optimus-0 / -1 (ViT-G/14 reg4) | 1536 | 1536 (CLS) | — |
| `H0miniEncoder` | bioptimus/H0-mini (CLS + mean patch) | 768 | 1536 | — |
| `ImageCLIPEncoder` | CLIP vision tower + projection | 768 | 512 | — |

Sources: [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L348-L366), [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L315-L343)

The default backbone deserves one architectural note: `MidnightEncoder` has a **three-way construction mode**. With `pretrained=True` it downloads upstream kaiko-ai/midnight weights; with `pretrained=False` it builds the architecture from a bundled `midnight_config.json` with random init — the mode used by `from_pretrained`, so the released checkpoint (which carries the fine-tuned backbone weights baked in) loads with no network access to the upstream repo. This is what makes the published model fully self-contained.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L315-L343), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L249-L289)

### LoRA as part of the architecture, not a wrapper detail

By default (`use_lora=True`), the freshly built backbone is immediately wrapped by PEFT's `get_peft_model`, with rank 8, α = 2r, dropout 0.2, targeting the modules the encoder declares. The class docstring codifies this as a **save/load contract**: the LoRA-wrapped structure is the model — state-dict keys carry the `backbone.base_model.model.` prefix, and the inference path must keep the wrapping (never `merge_and_unload()`), because a reconstructed `DeepSpotM(use_lora=True)` expects prefixed keys. When LoRA is off, the backbone is frozen explicitly instead — the ablation alternative to adapter training.

Sources: [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L11-L37), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L81-L95)

For the full prefix/reconstruction mechanics, continue to [LoRA Adaptation Contract](8-lora-adaptation-contract); per-backbone details are on [Pathology Vision Encoders](7-pathology-vision-encoders).

## The Decoding Stage: Genes as Queries, Not Outputs

The central architectural inversion of DeepSpotM is that **genes are decoder inputs, not output neurons**. A conventional expression-prediction head ends in `Linear(D, n_genes)`; here, each gene is a learned query vector that *attends to* the image's patch tokens, and the decoder is symmetric in batch and gene counts.

The decoder's forward pass is a fixed shape pipeline:

1. **Keys/values**: `patch_proj` maps patch tokens `(B, N, patch_dim)` → `(B, N, 256)`.
2. **Queries**: gene queries `(B, G, 256)` come from either the single-source path (`gene_embeddings` lookup + optional projection) or the multi-source path (active source's bio parameter → adapter → modality one-hot).
3. **Refinement**: `CrossAttentionLayer` × 2 — each gene query attends over all patches via `nn.MultiheadAttention`, followed by pre-norm residual + a 4×-expansion GELU FFN.
4. **Output**: per-gene head maps refined queries `(B, G, 256)` → `(B, G)` expression, plus mean-pooled gene features `(B, 256)` for downstream use.

Sources: [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L473-L520), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L43-L62), [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L713-L752)

Two consequences of the query design shape the rest of the API:

- **Selective prediction is free.** Passing `gene_indices` builds and cross-attends *only those queries*, so cost scales with `len(genes)` rather than the panel — this is exactly how `predict_genes(tile, ["EPCAM", "CD3D"])` becomes faster than a full forward.
- **Attention is interpretable per gene.** With `need_weights=True`, each layer returns `(B, heads, G, N)` attention; `get_gene_attention_maps` averages over heads of the last layer to give `(B, G, N_patches)` spatial maps — a per-gene localization of *where in the tile* that gene's evidence was found.

Sources: [modules.py](src/deepspotm/modules.py#L713-L729), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L397-L413), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L417-L454)

The full layer math and query-construction variants are detailed in [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder); the `gene_indices` shortcut in [Selective Gene Prediction](16-selective-gene-prediction).

## The Gene Representation Stage: Priors + Hypernetwork
