```mermaid
    A["User gene list<br/>['EPCAM', 'CD3D', 'PTPRC']"] --> B["model.predict_genes(pixel_values, genes)<br/>wrapped in @torch.no_grad()"]
    B --> C["model.genes_to_indices(genes)<br/>symbol → column index<br/>KeyError listing unknown symbols"]
    C --> D["model.forward(pixel_values, gene_indices=idx)"]
    D --> E{"Decoder type?"}
    E -->|"CrossAttentionGeneDecoder"| F["Slice at query construction:<br/>bio[gene_indices] / embedding lookup of selected rows"]
    F --> G["Cross-attention runs over<br/>B × G_sel × D queries only"]
    G --> H["Output head: router bio sliced<br/>by gene_indices"]
    H --> I["(B, G_sel) expression<br/>columns in requested order"]
    E -->|"MLP gene_head"| J["Full-panel linear head<br/>then index_select(1, idx)"]
    J --> I
```

Sources: [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L370-L391), [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L721-L724)

## The Python API: `predict_genes` and `genes_to_indices`

The public entry point is `DeepSpotM.predict_genes(pixel_values, genes)`. It accepts a single gene symbol (`str`) or a list of symbols, and returns a `(B, len(genes))` tensor whose **column order follows the input order** — not the vocabulary's canonical order. The method is decorated with `@torch.no_grad()`, so it is inference-only by construction and moves the index tensor onto the input's device before calling `forward`.

Symbol resolution is delegated to `genes_to_indices`, which performs a dictionary lookup against `_gene_to_idx` — a mapping built once in `__init__` from the ordered gene list loaded from `tokens.csv` (see [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping) for the vocabulary mechanics). Validation is strict: any symbol outside the model's panel raises a `KeyError` that lists up to ten offending names, so a typo like `EPCAN` fails loudly rather than silently producing wrong indices.

| API surface | Input | Output | Subset applied at | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `predict_genes(pixel_values, genes)` | gene symbol(s) as `str`/`list[str]` | `(B, len(genes))` tensor, input-ordered | Query construction (cross-attention path) | `KeyError` naming missing symbols |
| `forward(pixel_values, gene_indices=idx)` | 1-D LongTensor or list of ints | `(expression, gene_features, attn_weights)` triple | Query construction (decoder) / `index_select` (MLP head) | none — caller owns the indices |
| `model.gene_names` / `_gene_to_idx` | — | ordered panel / symbol→index dict | — | read-only reference data |

Sources: [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L406-L420), [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L393-L404), [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L72-L79)

## What Happens Inside the Decoder

Inside `CrossAttentionGeneDecoder.forward`, the `gene_indices` argument is first normalized — non-tensor inputs are converted with `torch.as_tensor(..., dtype=torch.long)` and then moved to the patch tokens' device. From that point, three stages respect the subset.

First, **query construction**. In single-source mode, the decoder embeds only the selected rows (`gene_embeddings(gene_ids)` where `gene_ids` is either the full `arange` or your `gene_indices`), applies `gene_query_proj` to those rows alone, and expands to the batch. In multi-source mode, `MultiSourceGeneEmbedding.forward` slices the trainable `bio_<source>` parameter (`bio[gene_indices]`) *before* the adapter projection — the code comments note this pre-expand ordering costs `G × bio_dim × D` rather than `B × G × bio_dim × D`, and slicing first compounds that saving. (The multi-source machinery itself is documented in [Multi-Source Gene Embeddings](11-multi-source-gene-embeddings).)

Second, **cross-attention**. The selected `(B, G_sel, D)` queries flow through every `CrossAttentionLayer`, so attention compute scales with `len(gene_indices)` instead of the full panel — the decoder docstring states this explicitly: *"only those gene queries are built and cross-attended, so cost scales with len(gene_indices) instead of the full panel."*

Third, **the output head**. When the router hypernetwork is active ([Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork)), its per-gene projection weights derive from the biological embeddings — so the router's bio input must be sliced too. The decoder does exactly that in both modes: `router_bio[gene_indices]` for the multi-source path and `bio_emb[gene_indices]` for single-source. Without this, the router would generate `n_genes` projection rows against only `G_sel` queries, and the `einsum` would fail on a shape mismatch.

> [!TIP]
> Subsetting is **numerically equivalent** to slicing the full output. `test_gene_indices_subset_the_output` asserts that a `gene_indices=[7, 1, 4]` call matches `full[:, wanted]` within `rtol=1e-4` — selective prediction changes *how much* is computed, never *what* the selected values are.

Sources: [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L713-L752), [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L411-L442), [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L421-L423), [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L775-L785)

## Selective Prediction from the Command Line

The CLI example script `examples/predict.py` exposes subsetting through `--genes GENE [GENE ...]`, described as *"score only these gene symbols instead of the full panel"*. The canonical usage from the script's own help text: `python examples/predict.py tiles/ --genes EPCAM CD3D PTPRC --output preds.csv`.

Internally, the batch loop branches on whether genes were requested: with `--genes`, each batch goes through `model.predict_genes(pixel_values, genes)`; without it, the full panel comes from `model(pixel_values)` and only the `--top N` highest-expression genes are printed per tile. Unknown symbols surface as the same `KeyError` from `genes_to_indices`, which `main()` catches and reports as `error: unknown gene symbol(s): ...` with exit code 1 — no partial CSV is written. When `--output` is set, the resulting CSV has tiles as rows and your requested genes as columns, in exactly the order you typed them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["predict.py invocation"] --> B{"--genes given?"}
    B -->|yes| C["model.predict_genes()<br/>selected queries only"]
    B -->|no| D["model(pixel_values)<br/>full panel"]
    D --> E["--top N ranking per tile"]
    C --> F["print 'gene=value' list<br/>in given order"]
    E --> G{"--output CSV?"}
    F --> G
    G -->|yes| H["DataFrame → CSV<br/>rows = tiles, cols = genes"]
    G -->|no| I["done"]
    C -.->|"KeyError on unknown symbol"| J["error: unknown gene symbol(s)<br/>exit 1"]
```

| CLI flag | Effect on selective prediction |
|---|---|
| `--genes GENE...` | Predicts only these symbols via `predict_genes`; output columns follow the given order |
| `--top N` | Ranks the full panel per tile; **ignored** when `--genes` is set |
| `--output CSV` | Writes the prediction matrix (tiles × genes); with `--genes`, columns are the requested subset |
| `--batch-size N` | Unchanged — batching is orthogonal; subsetting reduces work *within* each forward |

Sources: [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L62-L74), [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L103-L141), [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L169-L194), [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L18-L28)

## Cost and Correctness Guarantees

The savings are stage-by-stage and only materialize on the cross-attention architecture. The MLP head path accepts `gene_indices` purely for output-shaping convenience — it computes all `n_genes` columns and slices afterward, so there is no speedup. On the cross-attention path (the shipped configuration), every gene-proportional stage shrinks:

| Stage | Full panel (G genes) | Subset (g genes) | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bio slice / embedding lookup | materialize G rows | materialize g rows | `bio[gene_indices]` before adapter; embedding lookup of selected ids |
| Adapter projection (multi-source) | `G × bio_dim × D` (pre-expand) | `g × bio_dim × D` | slice-then-project compounds the documented pre-expand saving |
| Cross-attention (all layers) | `O(B × G × N × D)` | `O(B × g × N × D)` | only selected queries attend |
| Router output | einsum over G | einsum over g | `router_bio` sliced by `gene_indices` |
| MLP `gene_head` | `B × hidden × G` matmul | same, then `index_select` | **no saving** — post-hoc slice |

Correctness rests on two contract tests in `tests/test_decoder.py`, whose module docstring states the guarantee downstream integrations (such as TIAToolbox) rely on: *expression is (batch, n_requested_genes), and `gene_indices` both subsets and orders the columns*. One test asserts subset values match the sliced full panel; the other asserts that reversing the requested indices reverses the output columns.

> [!TIP]
> The returned `gene_features` triple element is the **mean over the selected queries only** (`gene_queries.mean(dim=1)`). If your pipeline consumes pooled slide-level features alongside expression, note that this vector is subset-dependent — mixing outputs from different `gene_indices` sets means the pooled features are not comparable across calls.

Sources: [test_decoder.py](/tests/test_decoder.py#L1-L8), [test_decoder.py](/tests/test_decoder.py#L57-L77), [modules.py](/src/deepspotm/modules.py#L787-L790)

## Related Capabilities and Where to Go Next

Selective prediction is deliberately distinct from three neighboring capabilities. **Vocabulary swapping** (`swap_gene_vocabulary`) *changes* the gene panel the decoder is built around — e.g., retargeting to a custom panel — which is checkpoint surgery, not a per-call filter; see [Cross-Vocabulary Checkpoint Handling](14-cross-vocabulary-checkpoint-handling). **Source selection** (`set_source`) chooses which embedding modality pathway is active in multi-source models; it composes orthogonally with `gene_indices`, and is covered in [Multi-Source Gene Embeddings](11-multi-source-gene-embeddings). Finally, `get_gene_attention_maps` accepts `gene_indices` too, but as a **post-hoc slice of full-panel attention** rather than query-level subsetting — useful for interpretability ([Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading) covers the loading context in which all of these run).

Suggested reading progression:

- For the mechanism behind per-gene queries: [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder), then [Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork)
- For the symbol→index mapping this page builds on: [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping)
- For running this end-to-end on tiles or slides: [Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools) and [Whole-Slide Image Pipeline](17-whole-slide-image-pipeline)


# Whole-Slide Image Pipeline



This page documents how DeepSpot-M turns a gigapixel whole-slide image (WSI) into a spatial gene-expression matrix. The pipeline lives in [`examples/predict_wsi.py`](examples/predict_wsi.py#L1-L231): it reads a slide with pyvips, lays a non-overlapping 224-px grid over it at native (~20x) resolution, discards background tiles with a two-stage filter, streams the surviving tissue tiles through the model in batches, and writes one spatial AnnData (`.h5ad`) per slide — the same format as the published TCGA virtual spatial transcriptomics atlas, ready for scanpy/squidpy. Unlike [`predict.py`](examples/predict.py#L2-L8), which scores pre-cut 224x224 tiles, this script owns the entire slide-to-data lifecycle: ingestion, tiling, filtering, inference, and spatial serialization.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L2-L14), [README.md](README.md#L99-L105)

## Pipeline at a Glance

The pipeline is a linear flow with two decision points: which slides to process, and whether to score the full ~19k-gene panel or a user-specified subset. Note the memory contract throughout — the slide is opened lazily and only `batch_size` tiles are ever held in RAM/VRAM at once, which is what makes gigapixel slides tractable on a single GPU.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input: slide.svs or folder of slides"] --> B["collect_slides: glob WSI_SUFFIXES"]
    B --> C["pyvips opens slide lazily, access=random"]
    C --> D["Stage 1: one-pixel-per-tile thumbnail<br/>flag candidates with mean ≤ white_mean + 10"]
    D --> E["Stage 2: crop each candidate at full resolution<br/>exact check: drop if mean > white_mean"]
    E --> F["Buffer PIL tiles + (x, y) coords until batch_size"]
    F --> G["image_processor: 224-px bicubic resize<br/>→ center crop → tensor → encoder normalization"]
    G --> H{"--genes given?"}
    H -- "yes" --> I["model.predict_genes(px, genes)<br/>selected gene queries only"]
    H -- "no" --> J["model(px) → full ~19k-gene panel"]
    I --> K["Concatenate expression chunks + tile coordinates"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["to_anndata: X, obs, obsm['spatial'], uns"]
    L --> M["Write <slide>.h5ad — scanpy/squidpy ready"]
```

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L79-L113), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L116-L136)

## Slide Ingestion and Format Support

The script accepts individual files or folders and recognizes the OpenSlide-family formats: `.svs`, `.tif`, `.tiff`, `.ndpi`, `.scn`, `.mrxs`, `.svslide`, and `.bif` (the `WSI_SUFFIXES` set). `collect_slides` expands inputs recursively (opt-out via `--no-recursive`), de-duplicates resolved paths, and returns a sorted list, so folder-of-slides runs produce deterministic output ordering. Slides are opened with `pyvips.Image.new_from_file(..., access="random")`, which keeps the pyramidal file on disk and satisfies `crop()` requests on demand — the ~1 GB slide in the tutorial never enters memory as a whole. Because tiles are cut at the slide's native pixel resolution, inputs should be ~20x H&E, the magnification DeepSpot-M was trained on.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L29-L44), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L86-L88), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L10-L11)

> [!TIP]
> Install the pipeline's dependencies with `pip install "deepspotm[wsi]"` — the `wsi` extra pulls in `pyvips>=2.2` and `anndata>=0.10`, which are deliberately excluded from the core package so tile-only users never need the libvips system library.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L57-L62), [README.md](README.md#L52-L57)

## Two-Stage Tissue Detection

Background rejection is the pipeline's performance lever: a melanoma slide can be over 90% white space, and every tile skipped is a forward pass saved. The `tile_slide` generator implements a two-stage filter that exploits the cost asymmetry between reading a thumbnail and reading full-resolution tiles:

| | Stage 1 — Thumbnail sweep | Stage 2 — Exact per-tile check |
|---|---|---|
| **Input** | One thumbnail pixel per tile column (resized to the `nx × ny` grid) | The full 224-px crop from the pyramid |
| **Computation** | `grid_mean` of the thumbnail, one `np.argwhere` | `arr.mean()` over the cropped tile |
| **Threshold** | `grid_mean ≤ white_mean + 10` | `arr.mean() > white_mean` → drop |
| **Cost** | One cheap pass per slide | One `slide.crop` read per candidate |
| **Purpose** | Prune the candidate set | Final decision per tile |

The +10 margin in Stage 1 is deliberate: the thumbnail pass is a *screening* step, so it errs toward keeping tiles (a tile slightly darker than the threshold at thumbnail scale might still be tissue at full resolution). Stage 2 then applies the authoritative `white_mean` test on real pixels. On the tutorial's TCGA-SKCM slide (99,960 × 65,991 px → a 446 × 294 grid), this cascade reduces 45,751 candidate tiles to 36,392 scored tissue tiles — roughly 20% pruned after the exact check alone, before any model compute.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L47-L76), [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L9-L31), [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L68-L79)

## Streaming Batched Inference

`predict_slide` consumes the `tile_slide` generator through an accumulator-and-flush loop: tiles and their `(x, y)` origins are buffered in plain Python lists, and when the buffer reaches `batch_size` (default 64), `flush()` stacks the tiles through `image_processor` — the encoder's eval transform, which bicubic-resizes to 224 px, optionally center-crops, converts to a tensor, and applies the encoder's normalization statistics — then runs a `torch.no_grad()` forward and appends the float32 CPU result to `chunks`. The gene-selection branch mirrors the model's public API: with `--genes`, the buffered tensor goes to `model.predict_genes(px, genes)`, which builds cross-attention only for the requested gene queries (three marker genes cost a fraction of the full panel); without it, `model(px)` returns the full `(n_tiles, ~19k)` panel whose column order is `model.gene_names`. The same flush pattern is what bounds memory: peak RAM holds one batch of PIL tiles, peak VRAM one batch of tensors, regardless of slide size.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L79-L113), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L406-L420), [model.py](src/deepspotm/model.py#L370-L391), [utils.py](src/deepspotm/utils.py#L26-L74)

> [!TIP]
> In the tutorial the same pattern is reproduced with one caveat: `import pyvips` must happen *before* `import torch` (libvips/glib initialization order). `predict_wsi.py` handles this implicitly — `main()` imports pyvips and anndata first and defers the `torch`/`deepspotm` imports until after dependency validation.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L33-L63), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L171-L202)

## Spatial AnnData Output

`to_anndata` packages predictions in the convention that downstream single-cell tooling expects. The expression matrix `X` holds predicted log1p-CPM values (rows = tissue tiles, columns = genes in prediction order); tile provenance lives in three AnnData slots:

| AnnData slot | Contents | Convention served |
|---|---|---|
| `adata.X` | `(n_tiles, n_genes)` float32 log1p-CPM expression | scanpy/squidpy standard |
| `adata.obs` | `x`, `y` columns; index `"{slide}_{x}_{y}"` | per-tile metadata, unique keys |
| `adata.obsm["spatial"]` | Tile *center* coordinates (`coords + tile/2`, float) | squidpy/scanpy `spatial` key |
| `adata.uns["deepspotm"]` | Slide filename, tile size, embedding source, `"log1p-CPM"` | provenance/reproducibility |

Because `obsm["spatial"]` stores tile centers in pixel space, `squidpy.pl.spatial_scatter` or the tutorial's matplotlib overlay places predictions correctly on the H&E with no rescaling logic on the consumer side. The `main()` loop writes one `.h5ad` per slide (or directly to `--output` when a single slide is given), skipping slides that raise `KeyError` for unknown gene symbols or yield zero tissue tiles — in both cases reporting the fix (check gene spelling, raise `--white-mean`) and exiting with a non-zero return code.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L116-L136), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L204-L226)

## CLI Reference

All knobs are exposed through argparse; defaults match the model's training regime and the tutorial's verified configuration:

| Parameter | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `inputs` (positional) | required | Slide file(s) or folder(s) of slides |
| `--output / -o` | `.` | `.h5ad` path (single slide) or output directory |
| `--repo` | `ratschlab/DeepSpotM` | HF repo id or local model directory |
| `--source` | `scgpt` | Gene-embedding source: `evo2`, `orthrus`, `prott5`, `scgpt`, `apertus` |
| `--genes` | none (full panel) | Score only these symbols (orders output columns) |
| `--tile` | `224` | Grid tile size in pixels |
| `--batch-size` | `64` | Tiles per forward pass |
| `--white-mean` | `220.0` | Mean-pixel threshold above which a tile is background |
| `--no-recursive` | off | Don't descend into sub-folders |
| `--device` | auto (`cuda` if available) | Force `cuda` or `cpu` |

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L139-L168), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L16-L22)

## Tile Pipeline vs Slide Pipeline

DeepSpot-M ships two sibling entry points that share the same model interface (`from_pretrained` → `image_processor` → `predict_genes`/`forward`) but diverge at I/O and filtering policy:

| Aspect | [`predict.py`](examples/predict.py#L1-L209) (tiles) | [`predict_wsi.py`](examples/predict_wsi.py#L1-L231) (slides) |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Pre-cut 224x224 tiles (`.png`, `.jpg`, …) | Pyramidal WSIs via pyvips |
| Tiling | Caller's responsibility | 224-px grid at native resolution |
| Background filtering | Opt-in (`--skip-background`) | Always on, two-stage |
| Output | Per-tile top-N printout or CSV | Spatial AnnData `.h5ad` with coordinates |
| Default batch size | 16 | 64 |
| Ecosystem | Quick inspection, pipelines over pre-chipped data | scanpy/squidpy spatial analysis, atlas-compatible |

The CSV output of `predict.py` lacks spatial coordinates by construction — it never knows where a tile came from — which is precisely the gap `predict_wsi.py` closes with its coordinate bookkeeping.

Sources: [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L103-L141), [predict.py](examples/predict.py#L83-L91), [predict_wsi.py](examples/predict_wsi.py#L4-L8)

## End-to-End Walkthrough: TCGA-SKCM

The tutorial notebook [examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L1-L31) executes this exact pipeline by hand on an open-access melanoma slide downloaded from the GDC portal with MD5 verification. It loads the released model with `source="scgpt"`, scores three compartment markers — `BRAF` (tumour), `CD37` (immune infiltrate), `COL1A1` (stroma) — across the 36,392 kept tiles, and overlays per-gene expression on a 2000-px slide thumbnail by scaling tile centers to overview coordinates. The notebook also documents the honest caveat that atlas figures were produced with cancer-finetuned models, so the base model's zero-shot maps look softer. For the guided, executable version of this walkthrough, see the dedicated tutorial page.

Sources: [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L9-L31), [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L95-L113), [predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb](examples/predict_tcga_skcm.ipynb#L221-L279)

## Where to Go Next

The WSI pipeline is a thin orchestration layer over deeper subsystems, each documented separately. To understand what happens to each tile *inside* the model — patch tokenization, LoRA adaptation, cross-attention decoding — start with [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview). The preprocessing step applied per tile (`image_processor`: resize → center-crop → normalize) is unpacked in [Image Preprocessing Transforms](18-image-preprocessing-transforms). The gene-subset fast path (`--genes` → `predict_genes`) is specified in [Selective Gene Prediction](16-selective-gene-prediction), and the loading contract behind `from_pretrained` in [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading). For a working command-line companion that scores already-cut tiles, see [Command-Line Prediction Tools](3-command-line-prediction-tools); for the notebook counterpart of this page, see [TCGA-SKCM Tutorial Notebook](4-tcga-skcm-tutorial-notebook).


# Image Preprocessing Transforms



Every image that reaches a DeepSpotM vision encoder must pass through a deterministic preprocessing pipeline: it must arrive as a tensor with the exact spatial size the encoder expects and pixel values standardized with the exact mean/std statistics the encoder was trained with. This page explains how that pipeline is built, who owns its configuration, and how it is wired into every inference path. The implementation lives almost entirely in two files — a generic factory in `src/deepspotm/utils.py` and encoder-specific normalization constants in `src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py` — with consumer wiring in `model.py`, `checkpoint.py`, and the example scripts.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L1-L75), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L1-L380)

## Why Normalization Is Encoder-Owned

DeepSpotM does not hardcode one preprocessing recipe. Each vision backbone — UNI, H-optimus, CLIP, Midnight — was pretrained with a different pixel standardization scheme, and feeding it tiles normalized with the wrong statistics silently degrades feature quality. The design therefore assigns every encoder subclass two class attributes, `NORM_MEAN` and `NORM_STD`, declared as a contract on the `ImageEncoder` base class ("Image normalization — every subclass must set these"). The encoder knows its own statistics; the transform factory only knows how to *apply* whatever statistics it is handed.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L34-L52), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L156-L159)

This separation produces a clean dependency direction: `image_encoder.py` imports the factory functions from `utils.py`, builds one transform pipeline per encoder at construction time, and stores it as `self.transforms`. Nothing else in the codebase needs to know which statistics belong to which backbone — a caller simply calls the callable stored on the encoder.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L1-L3), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L127-L140)

The transform-relevant code is concentrated in a small set of files:

```
src/deepspotm/
├── utils.py           # get_normalize_params + get_eval_transforms (the factory)
├── image_encoder.py   # per-encoder NORM_MEAN/NORM_STD, set_transforms, registry
├── model.py           # DeepSpotM.set_eval_transforms (PEFT-aware rebuild)
└── checkpoint.py      # load_for_prediction: switches to center-crop at predict time
examples/
├── predict.py         # applies image_processor to tile files
└── predict_wsi.py     # applies image_processor to whole-slide tiles
tests/
└── test_utils.py      # behavioral contract for the pipeline
```

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L1-L75), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L34-L52)

## The Anatomy of `get_eval_transforms`

The single factory function `get_eval_transforms(mean, std, target_img_size=-1, center_crop=False)` assembles a `torchvision.transforms.Compose` pipeline in four ordered stages. Understanding this order matters because each stage assumes a specific input format: stages 1–2 operate on PIL images, stage 3 produces a tensor, and stage 4 standardizes tensor values.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L27-L31)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Raw input<br/>(NumPy / PIL / tensor)"] --> B["Stage 1: ensure_pil<br/>coerce to PIL uint8"]
    B --> C{"target_img_size > 0?"}
    C -- "yes" --> D["Stage 2a: Resize(size)<br/>BICUBIC, aspect-preserving"]
    D --> E{"center_crop?"}
    C -- "no" --> F{"center_crop?"}
    E -- "yes" --> G["Stage 2b: CenterCrop(size)"]
    E -- "no" --> H["Stage 3: ensure_tensor<br/>ToTensor → float [0,1]"]
    G --> H
    F -- "yes: assert fails" --> X["AssertionError"]
    F -- "no" --> H
    H --> I{"mean and std given?"}
    I -- "yes" --> J["Stage 4: Normalize(mean, std)"]
    I -- "no" --> K["output stays in [0,1]"]
    J --> L["tensor (3, 224, 224)"]
    K --> L
```

| Stage | Operation | Trigger condition | Output state |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ensure_pil` lambda | always | PIL image, `uint8`, HWC layout |
| 2a | `Resize(size, InterpolationMode.BICUBIC)` | `target_img_size > 0` | shorter side resized to `target_img_size` |
| 2b | `CenterCrop(size)` | `center_crop=True` (asserts 2a ran) | square `size × size` image |
| 3 | `ensure_tensor` lambda | always | `float32` tensor, values scaled to `[0, 1]` |
| 4 | `Normalize(mean, std)` | both `mean` and `std` are not `None` | standardized tensor |

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L34-L75)

Two details deserve attention for beginners. First, torchvision's `Resize` with an integer argument resizes only the *shorter* side to that value while preserving aspect ratio — so a 256×300 tile becomes 224×263 before an optional `CenterCrop(224)` trims the longer dimension from the middle. That is why both the tile CLI and the checkpoint loaders ultimately run with `center_crop=True`: the encoder demands exactly 224×224. Second, the composition is built once and reused — the returned `Compose` object is a callable you apply per image, not a class you instantiate per batch.

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L56-L61), [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L53-L56)

## Input Coercion: One Pipeline for NumPy, PIL, and Tensors

Real-world producers of pathology tiles disagree on formats: slide-reading libraries hand over channel-last `uint8` NumPy arrays, some code paths carry tensors, and the package's own examples pass PIL images. Rather than forcing every caller to convert first, stage 1 (`ensure_pil`) accepts all three and raises a `TypeError` for anything else — the test suite's module docstring states this explicitly: "`get_eval_transforms` is the boundary every downstream integration crosses."

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L34-L53), [test_utils.py](/tests/test_utils.py#L1-L6)

| Input type | Handling in stage 1 | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `np.ndarray`, `uint8` | passed straight to `Image.fromarray` | PIL uint8 |
| `np.ndarray`, float | scaled by 255, clipped, cast to uint8 | PIL uint8 |
| `torch.Tensor` (CHW, float) | moved to CPU, `CHW → HWC` permute, ×255, clipped to uint8 | PIL uint8 |
| `PIL.Image.Image` | returned unchanged | PIL passthrough |
| anything else | `TypeError("Unsupported input type: ...")` | loud failure |

Sources: [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L34-L53)

The tensor branch deserves a closer look for beginners: a channel-first tensor of shape `(3, H, W)` with float values in `[0, 1]` — the format torchvision's `ToTensor` produces — is detected by checking `x.shape[0] in (1, 3)`, permuted to height-width-channel order, and quantized back to 8-bit pixels. The parametrized test then proves all four accepted input shapes converge to the identical output: a `float32` tensor of shape `(3, 224, 224)`.

Sources: [test_utils.py](/tests/test_utils.py#L19-L42)

## Normalization Constants Across the Encoder Registry

Each encoder in the registry pairs its architecture with the statistics its upstream pretraining used. The constants are defined once at module level and referenced by subclasses:

| Encoder | `NORM_MEAN` / `NORM_STD` source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `UNI1Encoder`, `UNI2Encoder` | ImageNet `(0.485, 0.456, 0.406)` / `(0.229, 0.224, 0.225)` | classic torchvision ImageNet stats |
| `H0miniEncoder`, `H0Encoder`, `H1Encoder` | Bioptimus `(0.707223, 0.578729, 0.703617)` / `(0.211883, 0.230117, 0.177517)` | H-optimus / Virchow-family stats |
| `ImageCLIPEncoder` | OpenAI CLIP `(0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073)` / `(0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711)` | may be overridden by checkpoint processor (see below) |
| `MidnightEncoder` | `(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)` for both mean and std | plain centering to `[-1, 1]` |

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L156-L159), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L162-L169), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L250-L254), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L301-L304)

The CLIP encoder adds a refinement on top of the contract: during `_build`, it attempts to load a Hugging Face `AutoImageProcessor` from the weights directory and, if that processor declares `image_mean`/`image_std`, those values **replace** the class defaults before the transform is built. The comment explains why — it "covers fine-tuned CLIP variants with custom norms." This is also the consumer of the second utility in `utils.py`, `get_normalize_params`, which extracts statistics from three shapes of object: a torchvision `Compose` pipeline (scanning for a `Normalize` step), a plain dict with `image_mean`/`image_std` keys, or any object carrying those attributes.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L276-L290), [utils.py](/src/deepspotm/utils.py#L8-L24)

> [!TIP]
> The CLIP override assigns to `type(self).NORM_MEAN` and `type(self).NORM_STD` — class attributes, not instance attributes ([image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L282-L284)). Constructing an `ImageCLIPEncoder` with a checkpoint that ships custom processor stats therefore mutates the class-level defaults process-wide. Harmless for the single-encoder workflows in this repo, but worth knowing if you instantiate multiple CLIP variants in one process.

## Rebuilding Transforms at Predict Time

Transforms are constructed once per encoder during `_build` — for timm-based encoders, right after weights are resolved and loaded, always with `target_img_size=224`. But two inference loaders deliberately *rebuild* the pipeline afterwards, because evaluation uses a stricter geometry than construction-time defaults: both call `set_eval_transforms(center_crop=True)` immediately before returning the model.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L136-L140), [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L329-L331), [checkpoint.py](/src/deepspotm/checkpoint.py#L182-L183)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as load_for_prediction / from_pretrained
    participant Model as DeepSpotM
    participant PEFT as PEFT wrappers (PeftModel → LoraModel)
    participant Enc as ImageEncoder
    participant Factory as get_eval_transforms

    Caller->>Model: build / load checkpoint
    Model->>Enc: build_encoder(...) — _build creates initial transforms
    Enc->>Factory: get_eval_transforms(NORM_MEAN, NORM_STD, target_img_size=224)
    Caller->>Model: set_eval_transforms(center_crop=True)
    Model->>PEFT: unwrap via base_model / model attributes
    PEFT->>Enc: reach the real encoder
    Enc->>Factory: set_transforms → rebuild pipeline with center_crop
    Enc-->>Caller: return (model, model.backbone.transforms)
```

Sources: [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L352-L365), [checkpoint.py](/src/deepspotm/checkpoint.py#L89-L99)

The `DeepSpotM.set_eval_transforms` method is the PEFT-aware entry point. When LoRA is enabled, `self.backbone` is not the encoder itself but a chain of wrappers (`PeftModel` → `LoraModel` → `ImageEncoder`); the method walks the chain explicitly by following `base_model`/`model` attributes until it finds an object exposing `set_transforms`, then delegates. The code comments that this explicitness guards against a future PEFT release breaking attribute delegation silently. At the encoder level, `set_transforms` merges any keyword arguments with the stored `build_kwargs` and calls the same factory — the model is untouched, only the transform pipeline is replaced.

Sources: [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L352-L365), [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L62-L68)

Both public loaders follow the identical closing ritual: move to device, switch to eval, rebuild transforms with `center_crop=True`, and return the tuple `(model, model.backbone.transforms)`. The docstrings name this second element `image_processor` — that is the callable the example scripts invoke per tile.

Sources: [model.py](/src/deepspotm/model.py#L329-L331), [checkpoint.py](/src/deepspotm/checkpoint.py#L182-L183)

> [!TIP]
> Always treat the returned `image_processor` as the single source of truth for feeding images to the model — never hand-roll a `Compose` yourself. It encodes the encoder-specific statistics, the 224-px contract, and the eval-time center-crop in one object; replicating any of the three by hand is the most common way beginners produce silently wrong predictions.

## Transforms Inside the Inference Entry Points

The tile-based script `predict.py` demonstrates the minimal integration loop: it opens each image file with PIL, converts to RGB, applies an optional background filter, and then hands the PIL image to `image_processor`. Note the ordering — background tiles are rejected *before* the transform runs, so no resize/normalize compute is wasted on blank glass:

```python
image = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
if white_mean is not None and float(np.asarray(image).mean()) > white_mean:
    continue                                   # skip background before transforming
batch_tiles.append(image_processor(image))     # the pipeline from utils.py
```

Sources: [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L130-L134), [predict.py](/examples/predict.py#L161-L162)

The whole-slide script `predict_wsi.py` follows the same pattern at larger scale. It cuts the slide into tiles on a 224-pixel grid at native resolution (default `--tile 224`), applies a two-stage background filter — a cheap one-pixel-per-tile thumbnail flags candidate tissue regions, then each candidate is re-checked at full resolution against `--white-mean` — and only surviving PIL tiles are transformed in the batch `flush()` step via `torch.stack([image_processor(im) for im in buf_imgs])`. Both scripts therefore rely on stage 1's PIL passthrough: the images they feed are already PIL, and the coercion lambda returns them unchanged.

Sources: [predict_wsi.py](/examples/predict_wsi.py#L47-L76), [predict_wsi.py](/examples/predict_wsi.py#L95-L95), [predict_wsi.py](/examples/predict_wsi.py#L157-L163)

## Behavior Guarantees from the Test Suite

`tests/test_utils.py` pins the pipeline's contract so refactors cannot silently change what models see. Each test maps to a guarantee you can rely on as a consumer:

| Test | Guarantee |
|---|---|
| `test_accepts_every_input_type` | NumPy uint8, NumPy float, PIL, and CHW tensors all produce a `(3, 224, 224)` `float32` tensor |
| `test_rejects_unsupported_input` | non-image inputs raise `TypeError` instead of failing downstream |
| `test_normalization_is_applied` | with stats: output standardized; with `None` stats: output stays in `[0, 1]` (verified against the exact value `128/255` for a uniform gray tile) |
| `test_center_crop_requires_a_size` | `center_crop=True` without `target_img_size` is an `AssertionError` at pipeline-build time |
| `test_get_normalize_params_*` | stats recovery works for `Compose` pipelines, pipelines without `Normalize` (returns `(None, None)`), and HF-style processor dicts |

Sources: [test_utils.py](/tests/test_utils.py#L19-L58), [test_utils.py](/tests/test_utils.py#L61-L95)

## Hands-On: Getting a Transform Without Weights

If you need to preprocess tiles to DeepSpotM's expected format without loading any model — for example to build a dataset cache or inspect tiles the way the encoder would — use the factory-level helper `build_encoder_transforms`, exported from the package root. It looks up the encoder class in the registry, reads its `NORM_MEAN`/`NORM_STD`, and calls the same `get_eval_transforms` with `target_img_size=224` — no timm import, no weight download, no model construction:

```python
from deepspotm import build_encoder_transforms

processor = build_encoder_transforms("H0Encoder", center_crop=True)
tensor = processor(pil_tile)   # ready-to-encode (3, 224, 224)
```

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L369-L379), [__init__.py](/src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L12-L26)

Passing an unknown encoder name raises a `ValueError` listing the available registry keys, mirroring `build_encoder`'s behavior — a useful safety net when experimenting with encoder names.

Sources: [image_encoder.py](/src/deepspotm/image_encoder.py#L348-L366)

## Where to Go Next

To see where these transformed tensors go next, follow the pipeline downstream: [Pathology Vision Encoders](7-pathology-vision-encoders) explains the encoder classes that own the normalization constants you met here; [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading) details the loading paths that trigger the center-crop rebuild; and [Whole-Slide Image Pipeline](17-whole-slide-image-pipeline) covers the tiling and background-filtering stages that run *before* the transform in `predict_wsi.py`. For how the transform contract is verified in CI, continue to [Test Suite and Packaging](19-test-suite-and-packaging).

# Test Suite and Packaging



DeepSpotM ships as a standard Python wheel whose correctness is enforced by a deliberately **checkpoint-free test suite**: because the pretrained weights are gated, every test is designed to verify guarantees that hold *without* ever downloading them. This page explains how the package is built, what the five test files guarantee on top of it, and why the testing strategy is shaped the way it is.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L87), [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L1-L7)

## Packaging Architecture: A src-Layout Wheel with Shipped Data

The build is plain setuptools, pinned to **`setuptools>=77`** for a specific reason: PEP 639. That standard introduced the machine-readable `license` and `license-files` fields, which the project uses to encode its dual-licensing scheme directly into distribution metadata — `PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0` for the code, with `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md` and `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md` shipped alongside so license terms travel with the artifact itself.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L4), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L11-L14), [Licensing and Research Use](20-licensing-and-research-use)

The distribution uses a **src layout**: `tool.setuptools.packages.find` searches only under `src/`, which makes it impossible for a test to accidentally import the source tree instead of the installed package — a property the packaging tests actively depend on. Crucially, the `package-data` directive ships `assets/*.csv` and `assets/*.json` into the wheel, so the gene vocabulary (`tokens.csv`), the Ensembl-to-symbol mapping (`ensp_to_gene.csv`), and the encoder configuration (`midnight_config.json`) travel with the code rather than being reconstructed at runtime.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L79-L83)

| Configuration field | Value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Name / version | `deepspotm` / `1.0.0` | Asserted by `test_version_is_installed` |
| `requires-python` | `>=3.10` | torch, transformers, peft, lightning all require ≥3.10; a 3.9 install cannot resolve a working dependency set |
| Build backend | `setuptools.build_meta` (≥77) | Enables the PEP 639 `license` / `license-files` fields |
| `license-files` | `LICENSE`, `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md`, `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md` | Dual code/weights licensing baked into the wheel |
| `packages.find` | `where = ["src"]` | src layout; tests exercise the installed package, not the tree |
| `package-data` | `assets/*.csv`, `assets/*.json` | Vocabulary and config data ship inside the wheel |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L6-L28), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L79-L83)

Dependency management follows a layered extras model: the core dependencies cover inference (torch, lightning, timm, peft, transformers), while optional extras scope heavier tooling to the workflows that need it. Note that `torchvision` — imported by the transform tests — is not declared directly; it arrives transitively through `timm`'s dependency chain.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L44-L55), [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L12-L14)

| Extra | Installs | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| `wsi` | `pyvips`, `anndata` | Whole-slide reading and AnnData export in `examples/predict_wsi.py` |
| `test` | `pytest>=7.0` | The test suite |
| `dev` | `test` + `wsi` + `build`, `ruff`, `twine` | Full development workflow including wheel building and linting |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L57-L71)

The flow from source tree to validated installation looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SRC["Source tree (src layout)"]
        CODE["src/deepspotm/**/*.py"]
        DATA["src/deepspotm/assets<br/>tokens.csv · ensp_to_gene.csv · midnight_config.json"]
    end
    subgraph WHL["Wheel deepspotm-1.0.0"]
        META["PEP 639 metadata<br/>license = PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0"]
        PKG["deepspotm package"]
        SHIP["package-data<br/>assets/*.csv, *.json"]
    end
    subgraph INST["Installed environment"]
        MD["importlib.metadata.version('deepspotm')"]
        API["deepspotm.__all__ — 12 names"]
        RS["importlib.resources.files('deepspotm.assets')"]
    end
    CODE --> PKG
    DATA --> SHIP
    PKG --> META
    PKG --> API
    SHIP --> RS
```

At runtime, packaged assets are resolved through **`importlib.resources.files()`**, never through source-tree paths. `config.py` builds `ALPHABET_PATH` from `files("deepspotm.assets")` with a filesystem fallback only as a last resort, and the inline comment documents why the deprecated `importlib.resources.path()` was avoided: it returns a context-managed path that is released on exit, so the stored value could outlive the guarantee it was valid.

Sources: [src/deepspotm/config.py](src/deepspotm/config.py#L7-L15)

> [!TIP]
> `importlib.resources.files()` returns a `Traversable` that stays valid for the process lifetime, whereas the deprecated `path()` hands back a `TemporaryDirectory`-managed path. Storing the latter in a class attribute (as `Config.ALPHABET_PATH` does) is exactly the bug class the comment guards against — the resource could vanish after the context manager exits.

## Testing Under Constraint: The Gated-Weights Problem

The pretrained weights live behind a gated Hugging Face repository, so an automated environment can never load a real checkpoint. The test suite turns this constraint into a design principle: rather than mocking the model, it tests **contracts** — shapes, types, orderings, and invariants — using a tiny randomly-initialised decoder, the packaged vocabulary, and pure functions over synthetic state dicts. The packaging test docstring states the philosophy explicitly: what can be guaranteed is that the package installs, that its public API is importable, and that the data files the model depends on actually ship in the wheel — *"Those are the failures that silently reach users."*

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L1-L7), [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L1-L8), [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    GATED["Gated pretrained weights<br/>(unreachable in CI)"]
    GATED -.->|"deliberately never loaded"| TS["pytest suite<br/>testpaths = tests"]
    TS --> P["test_packaging.py<br/>install · API · asset integrity"]
    TS --> D["test_decoder.py<br/>shape + ordering contract"]
    TS --> S["test_structure_expression.py<br/>packaged-vocabulary integration"]
    TS --> C["test_checkpoint.py<br/>guard logic on synthetic dicts"]
    TS --> U["test_utils.py<br/>input-type matrix"]
```

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L1-L7), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L85-L86)

Three complementary strategies emerge, each with a distinct verification boundary:

| Strategy | Representative tests | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Packaging contract** | `test_version_is_installed`, `test_asset_is_packaged` | Wheel installs; data files ship; metadata resolves | That the real weights load |
| **Small-model contract** | `test_forward_returns_the_documented_triple` | Shapes, dtypes, and orderings of the public API | Numeric quality of trained weights |
| **Guard unit tests** | `test_check_state_dict_load_rejects_unexplained_drift` | Failure modes raise loudly instead of silently degrading | End-to-end prediction correctness |

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L22-L24), [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L46-L54), [tests/test_checkpoint.py](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L55-L58)

## Test Suite Coverage Map

The five files partition cleanly along module boundaries. Each file's docstring doubles as a statement of which silent failure it exists to prevent:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph TESTS["tests/"]
        TP["test_packaging.py"]
        TC["test_checkpoint.py"]
        TD["test_decoder.py"]
        TSE["test_structure_expression.py"]
        TU["test_utils.py"]
    end
    subgraph PKG["src/deepspotm/"]
        INIT["__init__.py<br/>__all__ = 12 names"]
        CKPT["checkpoint.py"]
        MOD["modules.py"]
        CFG["config.py"]
        UT["utils.py"]
        ASSETS["assets/tokens.csv"]
    end
    TP --> INIT
    TP --> ASSETS
    TP --> CFG
    TC --> CKPT
    TD --> MOD
    TSE --> MOD
    TSE --> ASSETS
    TU --> UT
```

Sources: [src/deepspotm/__init__.py](src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L1-L31), [tests/](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L1-L6)

| Test file | Module under test | Technique | Headline guarantees |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_packaging.py` | Distribution metadata, `deepspotm.assets`, `config` | `importlib.metadata` / `importlib.resources` | Installed version; `__all__` importable; assets shipped and non-empty; vocabulary invariants |
| `test_checkpoint.py` | `deepspotm.checkpoint` | Synthetic state dicts | Prefix filtering; drift raises `RuntimeError`; allow-lists honoured |
| `test_decoder.py` | `CrossAttentionGeneDecoder` | Tiny randomly-initialised model, seeded with `torch.manual_seed` | Three-tuple return; `gene_indices` subsets *and* orders; attention path; modality registry consistency |
| `test_structure_expression.py` | `StructureExpression` | The packaged `tokens.csv` itself | 19 338 genes; placement by name; negative clamping; unknown genes ignored |
| `test_utils.py` | `get_eval_transforms`, `get_normalize_params` | Parametrised input-type matrix | numpy/PIL/tensor → `(3, 224, 224)` float32; loud `TypeError`; normalize-parameter extraction |

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L1-L64), [tests/test_checkpoint.py](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L1-L69), [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L1-L94), [tests/test_structure_expression.py](tests/test_structure_expression.py#L1-L55), [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L1-L96)

## The Packaging Contract: tests/test_packaging.py

Installability is checked first: `test_version_is_installed` asserts that `importlib.metadata.version("deepspotm")` resolves, proving the distribution — not just a directory of source files — is present in the environment. `test_public_api_is_importable` then parametrizes over `deepspotm.__all__` itself, so any of the twelve advertised names that fails to exist on the package fails a named test. This converts the `__all__` list from documentation into an enforced contract.

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L22-L32), [src/deepspotm/__init__.py](src/deepspotm/__init__.py#L20-L31)

Asset integrity is checked against the three data files the model depends on: each must exist via `importlib.resources.files("deepspotm.assets")` *and* be non-empty via `read_bytes()`. This is the direct backstop for the `package-data` glob — the classic silent packaging failure is a wheel that installs cleanly but ships without its data, which only surfaces as a user-side `FileNotFoundError`.

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L35-L43), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L82-L83)

The vocabulary test encodes the deepest invariant. `EXPECTED_GENES = 19338` ties `tokens.csv` to the model's reported output width — the module comment notes that a change to this file *is* a change to the model's output width. Two assertions follow: the count of rows with `token_type == "gene"` must equal 19 338, and token ids must form a **dense `0..n-1` range**, because the decoder indexes into them directly.

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L17-L19), [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L46-L56), [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping)

Finally, `test_config_alphabet_path_resolves` closes the loop between packaging and runtime: it asserts that `config.ALPHABET_PATH` — built from the `importlib.resources` chain — points at an existing file, proving the packaged-vocabulary resolution works from the installed distribution rather than only from a source checkout.

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L59-L63), [src/deepspotm/config.py](src/deepspotm/config.py#L8-L15)

> [!TIP]
> The dense token-id assertion (`ids == list(range(len(rows)))`) is load-bearing: the decoder treats `token_id` values as direct tensor row indices. A sparse or shifted id range would not raise anywhere — it would silently misalign every gene's output column, which is precisely the class of failure this suite is built to catch.

## Component Contracts Under Test

**Decoder contract.** Two seeded fixtures construct a miniature `CrossAttentionGeneDecoder` (12 genes, 16-dim patches) and a batch of patch tokens, so every test runs in milliseconds without network access. The assertions pin the API downstream integrations rely on: `forward` returns exactly the triple `(expression, gene_features, attn_weights)` with `attn` as `None` by default; expression is `(batch, n_requested_genes)` and finite; passing `gene_indices` computes *only* those columns and honours their requested order (verified by comparing a reversed index request against a flipped slice of the full output); and `need_weights=True` switches the third element to real per-layer attention.

Sources: [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L26-L43), [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L46-L77), [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder)

The registry test guards a subtler invariant: every source in `MODALITY_BY_SOURCE` must map into the canonical `MODALITY_VOCABULARY`, and position 0 must be `"dna"` — the module comment states the ordering is load-bearing because the index is what the one-hot encoding uses.

Sources: [tests/test_decoder.py](tests/test_decoder.py#L89-L93), [Gene Router Hypernetwork](10-gene-router-hypernetwork)

**Checkpoint-loading guards.** The docstring explains why these pure functions deserve tests: a regression in the drift guard "fails quietly and looks like a bad model rather than a bad load." The tests establish that `filter_state_dict` removes keys under vocab-specific prefixes while preserving everything else, and that filtering with an empty prefix tuple returns an *equal but distinct* dict (no accidental aliasing). For the guard itself: a clean load passes; unexplained missing or unexpected keys raise `RuntimeError` matching `"unaccounted-for key drift"`; and drift that the caller declared expected — via `allow_missing_prefixes` / `allow_unexpected_prefixes` set to `VOCAB_SPECIFIC_PREFIXES` — is permitted through.

Sources: [tests/test_checkpoint.py](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L1-L6), [tests/test_checkpoint.py](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L24-L40), [tests/test_checkpoint.py](tests/test_checkpoint.py#L48-L68), [Cross-Vocabulary Checkpoint Handling](14-cross-vocabulary-checkpoint-handling)

**Transform input matrix.** `get_eval_transforms` is described as "the boundary every downstream integration crosses": TIAToolbox hands it channel-last uint8 tiles, the WSI example hands it PIL images, and the model's own transform hands it tensors. A single parametrised test drives all four input flavours — numpy uint8, numpy float32, PIL, and CHW tensor — through the pipeline and asserts each emerges as a `(3, 224, 224)` float32 tensor. Complementary tests pin the failure mode (a string input raises `TypeError` rather than producing garbage), normalization behaviour (standardized when mean/std are given, `[0, 1]` when not), the configuration assertion that `center_crop` requires a positive `target_img_size`, and `get_normalize_params` extraction from a torchvision `Compose`, an empty pipeline, and a HuggingFace-style processor dict.

Sources: [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L1-L6), [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L26-L47), [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L56-L71), [tests/test_utils.py](tests/test_utils.py#L74-L95), [Image Preprocessing Transforms](18-image-preprocessing-transforms)

**Vocabulary integration.** `test_structure_expression.py` deliberately instantiates `StructureExpression()` with its default constructor, which resolves the packaged vocabulary — the docstring notes this "doubles as a check that the shipped tokens.csv is usable from an installed wheel rather than only from a source tree." The behavioural assertions cover placement by gene name (values land at vocabulary positions, the mask marks exactly the provided genes), clamping of negative expression values to zero, and isolation of unknown gene names, which must not shift or corrupt the output.

Sources: [tests/test_structure_expression.py](tests/test_structure_expression.py#L1-L5), [tests/test_structure_expression.py](tests/test_structure_expression.py#L12-L17), [tests/test_structure_expression.py](tests/test_structure_expression.py#L20-L44), [tests/test_structure_expression.py](tests/test_structure_expression.py#L47-L54)

## Running the Suite

Because `pyproject.toml` sets `testpaths = ["tests"]`, the standard workflow is an editable install followed by a bare `pytest` invocation. The `dev` extra bundles everything the suite and packaging workflow need; the `test` extra alone is sufficient if you only want to run the tests.

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"   # editable install + pytest + WSI extras + build/ruff/twine
pytest                    # discovers tests via testpaths = ["tests"]
```

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L57-L71), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L85-L86)

Each test is designed to diagnose its own packaging failure mode, so a red test points at a specific broken invariant:

| Failing test | Most likely cause |
|---|---|
| `test_version_is_installed` | Package not installed — running `pytest` from a source tree without `pip install -e .` |
| `test_asset_is_packaged` | A data file missing from `src/deepspotm/assets`, or the `package-data` glob no longer matching |
| `test_public_api_is_importable` | `__all__` advertises a name that no longer exists on the package |
| `test_token_vocabulary_matches_model_panel` | `tokens.csv` edited without re-deriving the 19 3338-gene panel width, or a non-dense token-id assignment |
| `test_config_alphabet_path_resolves` | Broken `importlib.resources` chain — assets present in source but absent from the installed distribution |

Sources: [tests/test_packaging.py](tests/test_packaging.py#L22-L63)

## Navigating Further

The contracts verified here anchor several deeper pages: the decoder triple tested in `test_decoder.py` is unpacked by the downstream tooling described in [Cross-Attention Gene Decoder](9-cross-attention-gene-decoder); the dense token-id invariant underpins [Gene Vocabulary and Output Mapping](12-gene-vocabulary-and-output-mapping); the drift guard is applied in [Cross-Vocabulary Checkpoint Handling](14-cross-vocabulary-checkpoint-handling); and the dual license metadata declared via PEP 639 is elaborated in [Licensing and Research Use](20-licensing-and-research-use). For the components these tests wrap at a conceptual level, start with [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview).


# Licensing and Research Use



DeepSpotM is released as a **research artifact**, and that intent is encoded in how the repository licenses its different parts. This page explains exactly what you may do with the code, the pretrained weights, and the third-party components they build on, what obligations follow from each, and how to cite the work correctly. Nothing here changes what the model does — it defines the legal and scholarly contract around it. If you have not yet run your first prediction, start with [Overview](1-overview) and [Quick Start](2-quick-start), then return here before redistributing or building on the model.

## Why One Repository Ships Two Licenses

Most repositories have a single `LICENSE` file; DeepSpotM deliberately does not. The project separates **artifacts** (things you run or redistribute) from **rights** (the terms attached to each), because code and model weights have different legal natures: source code is software, while weights are closer to a creative work that others fine-tune and share. The result is a split-license model with three files, each governing a different slice of the repository:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph ART["Repository artifacts"]
        CODE["Python source code<br/>src/deepspotm · examples"]
        W["Model weights<br/>model.safetensors"]
        FT["Your fine-tuned weights"]
        BB["Midnight vision backbone<br/>weights baked into model.safetensors"]
        EMB["Gene-embedding sources<br/>Evo 2 · Orthrus · ProtT5 · scGPT · Apertus"]
    end

    subgraph LIC["License files"]
        L1["LICENSE"]
        L2["WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md"]
        L3["THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md"]
    end

    CODE -->|"PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0"| L1
    W -->|"CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0"| L2
    FT -.->|"inherits CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0<br/>(ShareAlike)"| L2
    BB -->|"MIT — notice retained"| L3
    EMB -->|"MIT / Apache-2.0 — notices retained"| L3
```

The README states the split in two lines: code under PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, model weights under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, and the backbone and gene-embedding sources under MIT or Apache-2.0. Note the deliberate asymmetry: PolyForm places **no share-alike requirement on modified code**, but the CC license does impose share-alike on weight derivatives. That difference is the single most important thing to internalize before fine-tuning.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L180-L189), [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L17-L19)

A comparison across the three license layers:

| Artifact | License file | Commercial use | Derivative works | Core obligation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Source code | `LICENSE` | No | Allowed, any noncommercial purpose | Propagate terms + `Required Notice` |
| Model weights & fine-tunes | `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md` | No (incl. outputs) | Must stay CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 | Attribution + ShareAlike |
| Bundled third-party models | `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md` | Per their license | Per their license | Retain original notices |

Sources: [LICENSE](LICENSE#L1-L132), [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L1-L20), [THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md](THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md#L1-L15)

## The Code License: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0

`LICENSE` contains the full text of the **PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0**, a plain-language license family designed specifically for source code. Its central rule is that any *noncommercial purpose* is permitted. The text defines this generously rather than narrowly: personal research, experimentation, and testing for public knowledge, personal study, hobby projects, and amateur pursuits all qualify — as does use by charitable organizations, educational institutions, public research organizations, and government institutions **regardless of funding source**. That last clause matters in practice: an industry-funded lab at a public university is still covered.

Sources: [LICENSE](LICENSE#L52-L71)

What you *must* do under PolyForm is minimal but real. If you distribute the software (a fork, a patched build, an embedded copy), everyone who receives it must also receive the license terms or their URL, plus any plain-text lines beginning with `Required Notice:`. The license ships with a concrete example of the notice format: `Required Notice: Copyright Kalin Nonchev / ETH Zurich (https://github.com/ratschlab/DeepSpotM)`. You may modify the code and build new works from it for any permitted purpose, and the license even includes a patent grant covering claims the licensor can license — but it explicitly does **not** allow sublicensing your licenses to anyone else.

Sources: [LICENSE](LICENSE#L30-L38), [LICENSE](LICENSE#L40-L83)

Two boundary conditions complete the picture. First, if you are notified in writing that you violated the terms, you get a **32-day cure window**: come into full compliance and correct past violations within 32 days, and your licenses continue; otherwise they terminate immediately. Second, the software comes with no warranty and no liability — standard for research code, and worth remembering when outputs feed a downstream pipeline. Commercial use is simply not among the granted rights; the terms do, however, preserve the licensor's ability to grant separate licenses to others, which is the standard door for negotiating commercial use.

Sources: [LICENSE](LICENSE#L93-L108), [LICENSE](LICENSE#L78-L83)

## The Weights License: CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0

The pretrained model — `model.safetensors` and **any derived or fine-tuned weights** — is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International, with the full legal text linked from `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md`. The three letter terms translate into concrete obligations:

| CC term | Plain meaning | Practical requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **BY** (Attribution) | Credit the source | Credit DeepSpotM and cite the paper |
| **NC** (NonCommercial) | No commercial exploitation | Applies to the weights *and their outputs* |
| **SA** (ShareAlike) | Derivatives inherit the license | Fine-tunes must be released under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 |

Sources: [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L8-L15)

> [!TIP]
> Fine-tuning is where beginners get surprised: the moment you save a fine-tuned checkpoint, you have created a CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 derivative — even if you never modified a line of code. `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md` states this directly ("any derived/fine-tuned weights"), so any checkpoint you publish must carry the same license and credit the original work.

Also observe the NC scope: it covers "the weights **or their outputs**", meaning you cannot route weight-derived predictions into a commercial product any more than you could sell the weights themselves. This pairs with the code's PolyForm NC terms rather than conflicting with them — both layers refuse commercial use, so a compliant workflow must be noncommercial end to end.

Sources: [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L3-L6), [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L11-L12)

## Third-Party Components and Their Notices

DeepSpotM does not train its vision backbone from scratch, nor does it invent gene representations — it builds on six third-party foundation models, and `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md` records each one, its role, and its license. All six are **permissive** (MIT or Apache-2.0), which is why the project can redistribute their notices and bake backbone weights into its checkpoint:

| Component | Used as | License | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Midnight (`kaiko-ai/midnight`) | Vision backbone (weights baked into `model.safetensors`) | MIT | huggingface.co/kaiko-ai/midnight |
| Evo 2 | Gene embedding source (`bio_evo2`) | Apache-2.0 | github.com/ArcInstitute/evo2 |
| Orthrus | Gene embedding source (`bio_orthrus`) | MIT | github.com/bowang-lab/Orthrus |
| ProtT5 (`Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50`) | Gene embedding source (`bio_prott5`) | Apache-2.0 | huggingface.co/Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50 |
| scGPT | Gene embedding source (`bio_scgpt`) | MIT | github.com/bowang-lab/scGPT |
| Apertus (`swiss-ai`) | Gene embedding source (`bio_apertus`) | Apache-2.0 | huggingface.co/swiss-ai |

Sources: [THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md](THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md#L7-L14)

The embedding sources connect directly to the architecture: the gene router hypernetwork consumes frozen biological embeddings drawn from DNA, RNA, protein, single-cell, and text foundation models, as covered in [Multi-Source Gene Embeddings](11-multi-source-gene-embeddings) and [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview). For licensing purposes the takeaway is simple — permissive upstream licenses impose only notice retention, so they add no restrictions beyond the project's own split license.

Sources: [THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md](THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md#L1-L5)

## Research Use Only: Scope Boundary

Beyond licensing, the project draws an explicit **scope boundary**: a warning in the README — "Research use only. Not for clinical or diagnostic use." — appears before any usage instructions, and `CITATION.cff` repeats it in a software note alongside the license summary. This is not a licensing technicality but a deliberate positioning statement: predicted expression values are research signals, not diagnoses, and nothing in the release grants clearance for patient-facing use.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L44), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L21-L23)

The package metadata reinforces the same intent: the PyPI classifiers declare `Intended Audience :: Science/Research`, and the license comment in `pyproject.toml` reiterates that code is non-commercial only and that weights carry their own CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 license. If your use case drifts toward deployment rather than study, the repository is signaling — before you write any code — that you need different arrangements.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L11-L14), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L30-L32)

## How to Cite DeepSpot-M

Citation is the "Attribution" half of the weights license, and the project makes it machine-actionable. `CITATION.cff` is a standardized citation metadata file (the format GitHub uses to render its "Cite this repository" button) declaring the paper title, all five authors from ETH Zurich and the University of Zurich/Basel, version 1.0.0, the release date, and the DOI `10.64898/2026.06.19.26356060` for the medRxiv preprint. A `preferred-citation` entry pins the exact article record so citation tools resolve unambiguously.

Sources: [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L1-L24), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L41-L46), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L56-L81)

For LaTeX users, the README embeds a ready-to-paste BibTeX entry keyed `nonchev2026deepspotm`, and the README's Citation section restates the preprint link in prose. Practically: quoting either the BibTeX block or the CFF metadata satisfies the BY obligation on the weights.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L204-L222)

## Tracking Papers That Cite DeepSpot-M

The repository also maintains a living list of papers citing DeepSpot-M, updated **weekly via GitHub Actions** by `scripts/update_citations.py`. The script queries three independent scholarly APIs — Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, and OpenCitations — deduplicates results by DOI (then by normalized title), and merges them into an append-only store at `scripts/citations.json` before regenerating the "Papers Citing DeepSpot-M" section between `CITATIONS:START/END` markers in the README.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["DeepSpot-M DOI<br/>10.64898/...26356060"] --> B["scripts/update_citations.py<br/>(weekly GitHub Action)"]
    B --> S1["Semantic Scholar"]
    B --> S2["OpenAlex"]
    B --> S3["OpenCitations"]
    S1 --> D{"Deduplicate<br/>by DOI → title"}
    S2 --> D
    S3 --> D
    D --> E["scripts/citations.json<br/>append-only store"]
    E --> F["README.md<br/>Papers Citing section"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L191-L202), [scripts/update_citations.py](scripts/update_citations.py#L1-L24)

The design philosophy here is instructive for beginners: the store **never drops a paper** because an API failed — the docstring records a real incident where a Semantic Scholar outage shrank the visible list from 21 papers to 1 for a week. Requests retry on rate limits and server errors with exponential backoff, and if every source fails the script writes nothing and exits with status 1. Removing a false entry is a deliberate manual act (delete it from `citations.json`).

Sources: [scripts/update_citations.py](scripts/update_citations.py#L1-L24), [scripts/citations.json](scripts/citations.json#L1-L51)

## How Licenses Travel with the Package

Licensing survives installation. `pyproject.toml` uses the modern **PEP 639** packaging fields: an SPDX license expression (`license = "PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0"`) and a `license-files` list that ships all three legal documents — `LICENSE`, `WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md`, and `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md` — inside every built distribution. SPDX is the standardized identifier vocabulary for licenses, so tools reading package metadata see a machine-parsable license rather than a free-text string.

> [!TIP]
> Because `license-files` includes all three documents, anyone who installs `deepspotm` from PyPI receives the complete legal terms — including the weights license — without ever visiting the repository. PEP 639 support is why the build system pins `setuptools>=77`; older build backends silently ignore these fields, which would break license propagation.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L14)

This packaging contract complements the asset-shipping tests described in [Test Suite and Packaging](19-test-suite-and-packaging): CI verifies that the data files the model depends on reach users, while PEP 639 guarantees the legal files do the same.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L2-L3)

## Practical Compliance Checklist

The following table condenses everything above into the scenarios a beginner is most likely to face:

| If you… | Code (PolyForm NC) | Weights (CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0) | What you must do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Run inference for academic research | ✅ Permitted | ✅ Permitted | Cite the paper |
| Publish results in a paper | ✅ Permitted | ✅ Permitted | Cite (satisfies BY) |
| Fine-tune the weights | ✅ Permitted | ✅ Permitted | Release the checkpoint under CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (SA) |
| Fork / redistribute the code | ✅ Permitted | — | Include license terms and the `Required Notice` |
| Redistribute weights | — | ✅ Permitted | Credit + same license |
| Embed outputs in a commercial product | ❌ Not granted | ❌ Not granted (outputs included) | Seek separate permission from the licensor |
| Use clinically / diagnostically | ❌ Out of scope | ❌ Out of scope | Do not use |

Sources: [LICENSE](LICENSE#L52-L83), [WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md](WEIGHTS_LICENSE.md#L8-L19), [README.md](README.md#L44)

For any scenario in the last two rows, the contact path is documented: questions go to the first author via the README's Contact section, and the license texts themselves preserve the licensor's right to grant separate terms.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L224-L227), [LICENSE](LICENSE#L78-L83)

## Where to Go Next

Licensing is the outermost layer of the project's contract; the technical layers are documented across the catalog. To understand *what* you are licensing, read [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview) and [Pretrained Model Loading](13-pretrained-model-loading), which explain the checkpoint whose redistribution terms you just learned. To work with the released artifacts beyond local inference, [Atlas and Dataset Access](5-atlas-and-dataset-access) covers the gated TCGA virtual atlas on Hugging Face, whose access gating is a related (though separate) control mechanism. For the engineering conventions that keep the package — and its license files — shipping correctly, see [Test Suite and Packaging](19-test-suite-and-packaging).
